title: Foundation-model imaging biomarkers for pancreatic cancer: cross-species discovery of conserved tumour biology in mouse MRI and human CT.
abstract: Background Computed tomography (CT) stages pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) but does not read out the treatment-guiding tumour biology, requiring biopsy. Whether an imaging-biology relationship discovered in preclinical MRI holds independently in human CT is unknown. Methods One pipeline was applied to two PDAC cohorts: longitudinal 9.4 T multi-parametric MRI (169 sessions; 1002 image series, 471 quantitative maps) with terminal histopathology in male C57BL/6 mice bearing orthotopic KPC-derived tumours treated with gemcitabine, a dendritic-cell vaccine, both, or neither, and abdominal CT with matched proteogenomics from CPTAC-PDA. Radiomics and frozen foundation-model embeddings were modelled under grouped cross-validation against five pre-specified paired endpoints, with no cross-species transfer of features, weights, or labels. Findings Applied independently, the pipeline recovered four matched molecular endpoints in both species (CD8 infiltration, stromal collagen, CD8:CD68 immune balance, cytolytic activity), with areas under the receiver-operating-characteristic curve (AUROCs) of 0.938-0.960 in mice and 0.780-0.856 in humans. Survival concordance indices were 0.729 and 0.689. After adjustment for age, stage, and grade, the human imaging score remained independently prognostic (hazard ratio 1.87 per SD, 95% CI 1.32 to 2.66; p < 0.001 [Wald test]; combined concordance index 0.726 versus 0.611 for clinical covariates). Findings held in portal-venous-restricted analysis; frozen embeddings outperformed end-to-end fine-tuning in both arms. Interpretation One pipeline recovered matched PDAC biology in mouse MRI and human CT, supporting preclinical imaging to nominate non-invasive CT biomarker candidates for biopsy-sparing PDAC trial stratification, pending prospective external validation. Funding National Cancer Institute; Society of Interventional Radiology Foundation; University of California Irvine Anticancer Challenge Pilot grant.

One pipeline recovered matched PDAC biology in mouse MRI and human CT, supporting preclinical imaging to nominate non-invasive CT biomarker candidates for biopsy-sparing PDAC trial stratification, pending prospective external validation.

title: Mitral Annular Calcification - Association with Comorbidities and Left Ventricular Mechanics.
abstract: Aims Mitral annular calcification (MAC) is common in the general population, more pronounced in women and patients with left ventricular (LV) pressure overload conditions, which may increase stress on the mitral valve inducing and exacerbating the calcification process. The pathogenesis of MAC is presumed multifactorial but remains poorly understood. Women display a different LV response to pressure overload compared to men, but this association has rather not been thoroughly investigated. Methods and results The DANCAVAS (Danish Cardiovascular Screening) pilot study included randomly selected individuals from the general population aged 60-75 years to undergo a computed tomography (CT)-based screening program. MAC was graded by mitral valve calcification (MVC) score assessed by CT and compared to echocardiographic data. Among 463 participants, MAC was found in 165 (35.6%) with MVC scores ≤100 AU in 20.7%, 100-400 AU in 8.2% and >400 AU in 6.7%. While MAC was most prevalent in men, women presented with higher MVC scores and severe MAC on echocardiography. Patients with MAC were elderly with cardiovascular risk factors. Concentric LV geometry with smaller LV cavities and higher relative wall thickness were highly associated with MAC (p<0.001). From multivariable analyses, relative wall thickness and the mechanical load on the mitral valve (i.e. Stress MV ) strongly associated with MAC (SD-adjusted OR 28.8, 95% CI [15.6;53.5] and 2.97 [2.25;3.91], respectively) and MAC severity (10.9 [7.74;15.5] and 2.98 [2.33;3.82], respectively). The predictive performance was high with AUC of 0.78 [0.74;0.82] by including Stress MV in the model of age, sex and cardiovascular comorbidity (p<0.001). However, relative wall thickness had distinctive importance (AUC 0.96 [0.94;0.98], p<0.001) regardless of sex. Conclusion MAC is common in the general population with the highest prevalence among men. LV geometry and the pressure on the mitral valve are crucial factors in the pathogenesis of MAC, and sex-specific differences in LV response to pressure overload may elucidate why more extensive grades of MAC mainly affect women.

title: CT-based AI risk support for cystic renal masses: multicenter validation, reader study, and a randomized implementation study.
abstract: Background Cystic renal masses are frequently overtreated. We developed and evaluated the Kidney Imaging-based Triage Engine for Cystic Renal Masses (KITE-CRM), a computed tomography (CT)-based deep-learning pathway using artificial intelligence (AI) to support malignancy risk assessment in cystic renal masses (CRMs). Methods We conducted a multicentre development and validation study in China. In phase 1 (January 2020-December 2021), we developed the system in a retrospective training cohort from a tertiary referral center. CRMs were defined as renal lesions with predominantly cystic features. Corticomedullary-phase contrast-enhanced CT was the sole model input. In phase 2 (January 2022-October 2025), we externally validated the model across five independent hospitals. The core task was lesion-level malignancy discrimination; secondary tasks classified malignant lesions as clear-cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) versus other malignant subtypes and stratified ccRCC as high-grade versus low-grade disease. Retrospective cohorts comprised 3150 patients. The core task used 570 training cases (142 malignant), 235 internal-validation cases (137 malignant), and 528 external cases (160 malignant). Three-dimensional processing used one index lesion per patient and a fixed threshold of 0.586442888. In a randomized crossover multi-reader, multi-case study, six radiologists interpreted 117 external-cohort cases with and without AI; outcomes were area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC), sensitivity, specificity, reading time, and user acceptance. In phase 3 (November 2025-February 2026), 5869 eligible consecutive adults undergoing contrast-enhanced abdominal CT at Changhai Hospital were randomized 1:1 to AI-assisted (n = 2934) or standard reporting (n = 2935). The primary clinical endpoint was the proportion of pathologically benign lesions among treated lesions. The trial was registered with the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (ChiCTR2500112290); model code is publicly available. Findings Internal-validation AUROC was 0.996 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.990-0.999) and Brier score 0.046 (0.036-0.058). External AUROCs were 0.913-0.999, excluding Test 4 (AUROC 1.000; three malignant cases). External sensitivity ranged from 19/24 (79.2%) to 3/3 (100.0%) and specificity from 100/116 (86.2%) to 33/33 and 115/115 (100.0%). AI assistance increased reader-averaged AUROC from 0.825 to 0.973 (difference, 0.149; 95% CI, 0.091-0.206) and reduced mean interpretation time from 9.7 to 5.5 min. Benign pathology occurred in 28/171 (16.4%) treated lesions with AI versus 104/258 (40.3%) with standard care (difference, -23.9 percentage points; 95% CI, -31.7 to -15.4). The treated AI-evaluable CRM subgroup difference was non-significant (5/29 [17.2%] versus 19/56 [33.9%]; p = 0.105). In post hoc intention-to-treat analysis, benign intervention occurred in 28/2934 (0.95%) versus 104/2935 (3.54%) randomized participants (risk difference, -2.59 percentage points; 95% CI, -3.38 to -1.85; p < 0.0001). Median reporting time was 7.6 versus 18.5 min. Interpretation KITE-CRM improved assisted interpretation and reporting efficiency. Management findings do not establish long-term oncologic safety or CRM-specific clinical superiority. The model complements, rather than replaces, Bosniak assessment, indicated multiphase CT or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and clinical judgment. Broader prospective evaluation is needed. Funding National Natural Science Foundation of China and Shanghai municipal research programmes.

title: Technical benchmark of a high-speed ring gantry kV-CBCT imager for CBCT-based dose calculation.
abstract: Purpose A CBCT platform (HyperSight (HS)) mounted on an O-ring linac (ETHOS v1.1), is compared with standard CBCT imagers installed on C-arm (TrueBeam v2.7) and O-ring (Halcyon v3.0) linacs, as well as planning CT (pCT). The study focuses on image quality, radiation dose, and dosimetric evaluation (Hounsfield unit (HU) accuracy and dose comparison). Methods Phantom-based comparisons were performed using default CBCT protocols and reconstruction algorithms available (FDK, iCBCT and iCBCT Acuros CTS). Quantitative image quality metrics (noise, CNR, TTF, low contrast resolution) were studied (IQMetrix software). Radiation dose measurements were compared between CBCT platforms and against manufacturer values.pCT-CBCT HU comparisons were performed on HU-density calibration and anthropomorphic phantoms (Mean Error (ME) and Mean Absolute Error (MAE)). Dosimetric evaluations included relative dose deviations (D50%), and 3D gamma analysis. Results The HS imager demonstrated improved image quality and detection efficiency associated with a reduction in radiation doses compared to standard CBCT imagers. HU accuracy improved markedly for HS images reconstructed with iCBCT Acuros CTS yielding MAE(Body) < 29HU except for Head, and |ME (Soft tissue)| <8HU except for Large Pelvis protocol. For density calibration phantom, HU deviations remained within ± 50 HU except for bone densities. Dosimetric comparisons showed dose deviations below 0.5% between pCT and CBCT-based calculations for all protocols using HyperSight with iCBCT Acuros CTS (except for Large Pelvis (0.9%)). Gamma passing rates were consistently above 97.7% for 0.5%/1 mm criteria. Conclusion These results confirm the value of 125 kVp HS images reconstructed with iCBCT Acuros CTS for CBCT-based dose calculation.

title: Multicentre study of activity quantification methods for 99m-Tc-pyrophosphate SPECT/CT in cardiac amyloidosis.
abstract: Objective 99mTc-PYP SPECT/CT imaging is used for diagnosis of transthyretin cardiac amyloidosis (ATTR-CA). The calculation of quantitative metrics allows assessment of the myocardial amyloid burden and supports therapy response evaluations. This study explores the implementation of reliable metrics and the validation of activity quantification methods in a multicentre study. Methods As part of the IAEA Transthyretin Amyloid Cardiomyopathy (iTAC) project, a multicentre phantom study was conducted at 10 institutions using 12 hybrid SPECT/CT systems. Standardized acquisitions consistent with clinical protocols were used to compute the activity calibration factors (ACF). Absolute activity verifications were based on cardiac insert measurements with known activity distributions. Multiple reconstruction/quantification approaches (RecMethod) were evaluated, including the institution method (SiteProc) and four alternative ones; results of the computed activity were compared with the true activity meter measurements. Accuracy was assessed using RecMethod-to-True activity ratios, summarized by median, interquartile range (IQR) and coefficient of variation (CV). Results Most institution ACF values (ACF SiteProc ) ranged 75-105 cps/MBq and were consistent with reference CoreLab estimates. Agreement between ACF SiteProc and reference CoreLab values showed a median ratio of 99.6 %, IQR 5.8 %, and CV 9.4 %, indicating no systematic bias. For activity quantification, median RecMethod-to-True ratios were 100.1 % for the SiteProc reconstructions and 97.8 %, 94.1 %, 95.6 % and 96.0 % for the alternatives. Conclusion The evaluated quantification methods demonstrated good median accuracy across institutions providing reliable activity estimates, essential for a robust implementation of quantitative metrics for ATTR-CA. The obtained inter-site variability indicates that precision remains a challenge at the multicentre quantitative imaging studies.

title: An experimental imaging dose estimation method for the phase-II proton CT scanner.
abstract: Purpose Proton computed tomography (pCT) improves range accuracy in proton therapy by directly mapping proton stopping power relative to water (RSP). Imaging dose remains a crucial factor in determining the feasibility of daily image guidance. This study presents an experimental methodology for estimating imaging dose in the phase-II pCT scanner, utilizing phase space data recorded at the front tracker to eliminate phantom-specific corrections. The estimated doses are validated against ionization chamber (IC) measurements. Methods Dose measurements were conducted at multiple locations and angles within two phantoms, with data acquisition triggered by either the front trackers or the energy detector. Baseline scans were also performed without phantoms. Monte Carlo (MC) simulations were used to estimate imaging dose in single projections and full scans. Eight front-tracker-triggered baseline datasets were processed for proton track reconstruction and fluence estimation. After assessing inter-run variability, phase space files were averaged to generate an input source for MC simulations. The simulated imaging doses were renormalized to the averaged datasets and quantitatively compared against IC measurements. Results Analyzed proton track numbers exhibited consistency across datasets, with coefficients of variation below 2.0%. Estimated doses agreed with IC measurements within ±1.8% for the CTDI phantom; head phantom underestimated -4.6% (single projection) and -6.7% (full scan). Uncertainties from multiple measurements remained below 1.9%. Conclusion This study introduces a reliable workflow for imaging dose estimation in the phase-II pCT scanner. Purpose

Proton computed tomography (pCT) improves range accuracy in proton therapy by directly mapping proton stopping power relative to water (RSP). Imaging dose remains a crucial factor in determining the feasibility of daily image guidance. Baseline scans were also performed without phantoms. Monte Carlo (MC) simulations were used to estimate imaging dose in single projections and full scans. Eight front-tracker-triggered baseline datasets were processed for proton track reconstruction and fluence estimation. After assessing inter-run variability, phase space files were averaged to generate an input source for MC simulations. The simulated imaging doses were renormalized to the averaged datasets and quantitatively compared against IC measurements.

Analyzed proton track numbers exhibited consistency across datasets, with coefficients of variation below 2.0%. Estimated doses agreed with IC measurements within ±1.8% for the CTDI phantom; head phantom underestimated -4.6% (single projection) and -6.7% (full scan). Uncertainties from multiple measurements remained below 1.9%.

This study introduces a reliable workflow for imaging dose estimation in the phase-II pCT scanner. The approach demonstrates satisfactory agreement with IC measurements, supporting its feasibility for evaluating imaging dose in image-guided and adaptive proton therapy.

title: Minimum recommended distances between cardiac implantable electronic devices and the applicator surface in low-energy intraoperative radiotherapy of the breast: an in vivo dosimetric study.
abstract: Purpose Clinical guidelines recommend keeping the dose to cardiac implantable electronic devices (CIEDs) below 2 Gy. In low-energy intraoperative radiotherapy (IORT) of the breast, the Intrabeam treatment planning system (TPS) estimates dose in water, without accounting for tissue attenuation, reduced scatter at the skin surface and backscatter from tungsten shielding. This study aimed to determine conservative minimum recommended distances between the CIED and the applicator surface based on in vivo dosimetry. Materials and methods Thermoluminescent dosimeters (TLDs), cross-calibrated against an ionization chamber, were placed on the skin between the applicator and the infraclavicular region, close to the usual CIED location, in 21 patients undergoing breast IORT. Applicator-to-dosimeter distances were measured with intraoperative ultrasound, and dose-distance curves were fitted to identify the distance at which dose falls below 2 Gy (d <2Gy ). Results Tungsten shielding increased the surface dose by approximately 22%, whereas without shielding the surface dose in water was on average 3% lower than predicted under full-scatter conditions. The median d <2Gy exceeded the TPS value by 3.1 mm (interquartile range -1.7 to 4.5 mm), with large inter-patient variability. Minimum recommended distances, defined as the upper 95% confidence limit of the regression of d <2Gy on applicator diameter, ranged from 29 mm (35 mm applicator) to 39 mm (50 mm applicator), compared with 22-24 mm calculated by the TPS. Conclusion Intraoperative ultrasound combined with applicator-specific minimum recommended distances provides a practical tool to guide treatment decisions in patients with CIEDs undergoing low-energy breast IORT.

title: PROton therapy for HPV-related oroPHaryngeal cancer patients using normal tissue complication probability (NTCP) modEl-based strategy: an iTalian multIcenter retrospective Cross-sectional study - PROPHETIC.
abstract: Background Intensity-modulated proton therapy (IMPT) has shown promise in reducing toxicityfor patients with oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma (OPSCC), while maintaining comparable tumor control to intensity-modulated radiation therapy (IMRT). However, technical, logistical and economic factors have limited widespread implementation. Methods We conducted the first Italian multicenter in-silico comparative study of photon and proton plans in 100 patients with HPV-related OPSCC, involving seven radiation oncology departments. Clinical photon-based plans (mostly using Volumetric Modulated Arc Therapy (VMAT)) were compared with robustly optimized IMPT plans generated using the CNAO beamline. Dosimetric endpoints and normal tissue complication probability (NTCP) values for xerostomia and dysphagia were assessed. Eligibility for IMPT was retrospectively estimated using the Dutch model-based selection (MBS)criteria. Results Target coverage was comparable between modalities, although IMPT plans showed slightly lower conformity indices. IMPT significantly reduced the dose bath to healthy tissues, with lower mean doses to the parotids, submandibular glands, pharyngeal constrictors, oral cavity, brainstem, and spinal cord (p < 0.01). NTCP analyses predicted clinically relevant reductions in xerostomia and dysphagia with IMPT. Applying the MBS approach, 36 % of patients were deemed eligible for PT, consistent with previous reports. Inter-center variability in eligibility reflected differences in delineation practices and clinical protocols. Conclusions This study tested the feasibility of a multicenter model-based evaluation for IMPT in Italy. A substantial proportion of OPSCC patients could benefit from IMPT, though results likely represent a conservative estimate due to protocol choices. Standardized delineation, robust optimization, and integration of NTCP models are essential for consistent patient selection.

title: Single prior-based 3D volumetric tracking from a planar snapshot in spine SBRT: A proof-of-concept study.
abstract: Background Continuous 3D onboard monitoring is essential to ensure accurate dose delivery of stereotactic body radiation therapy. However, current approaches for 2D-to-3D volumetric estimation typically require extensive patient-specific data, or depend on auxiliary imaging hardware. This study introduces a proof-of-concept framework for data-efficient, patient-specific 3D volumetric tracking using only a single volumetric prior. Methods A retrospective dataset of 80 spine SBRT patients was utilized. Digitally Reconstructed Radiographs synthesized from cone-beam computed tomography volumes served as surrogates for onboard kV projections. The pipeline consists of patient-agnostic pre-training using an archival dataset, patient-specific adaptation using the single volumetric prior supplemented by non-rigid motion simulations, and simulated intra-fractional 3D estimation. The network employs a modified Attention U-Net with a channel-to-depth bottleneck and a triple feature concatenation to map the 2D to 3D spatial domain. Results The proposed model demonstrated a statistically significant improvement in structural tracking capabilities compared to a static uncompensated baseline. Furthermore, the performance variance across patients was substantially compressed, enhancing reliability against setup uncertainties while achieving high spatial concordance in the complex spinal anatomy. The inference throughput reached approximately 10 frames per second. Conclusions This proof-of-concept study establishes the technical feasibility of data-efficient, patient-specific onboard volumetric tracking using a single volumetric prior by successfully resolving anatomical deformations from a single 2D projection in near real-time.

title: Efficient proton adaptive breast radiotherapy with CBCT-Based synthetic CT.
abstract: Purpose Repeat CTs (reCTs) are routinely used during breast proton radiotherapy to assess anatomical and positioning changes; however, they increase patient dose and workflow burden. This study evaluated CBCT-based synthetic CT imaging for accurately monitoring fractional dose distribution and developed an adaptive workflow for breast proton therapy. Methods A retrospective analysis included 26 breast cancer patients who received both CBCT and reCT on the same day between 2022 and 2024. Two commercial synthetic CT algorithms were studied: corrected CBCT (corrCBCT), which utilizes iterative correction, and virtual CT (vCT), generated by deforming the planning CT to match the CBCT. Treatment plans were recalculated on the corrCBCT and vCT, and compared with same-day reCT metrics. A prospective evaluation of weekly vCT-guided dosimetry was performed in an additional 25 patients to assess its feasibility in adaptive workflows. Results CorrCBCT and vCT produced reliable dosimetric results when compared with reCT. Target coverage, measured by the mean percentage dose difference in D95% to the breast or chest wall, was -0.80% (SD = 1.3) for the corrCBCT and -0.7% (SD = 1.6) for the vCT. vCT also showed good agreement with same-day reCT imaging for dose metrics of adjacent critical structures. Larger discrepancies were observed in nodal targets, primarily due to CBCT image artifacts in the shoulder region. Conclusion Accurate proton-dose calculations require reCT, but synthetic CT can effectively flag tissue alterations. This study shows that monitoring dosimetric shifts from vCT can prompt targeted reCT-based replanning in unilateral breast proton therapy, thereby sparing patients the exposure and logistics of routine reCT during treatment.

title: CT-ED/MD calibration curve commissioning and end-to-end validation of HyperSight CBCT-Based dose calculation for online adaptive radiotherapy.
abstract: Purpose To establish a CT number-to-electron/mass density (CT-ED/MD) calibration curve for the HyperSight cone-beam CT (CBCT) system on the Ethos platform, perform end-to-end dosimetric validation, and evaluate whether a single curve applies across kV imaging energies. Methods An electron density phantom (CIRS 062 M) was scanned at 125 and 140 kV and reconstructed using iterative CBCT (iCBCT) Acuros and metal artifact reduction (MAR) algorithms. A 125-kV curve was generated from the averaged Acuros/MAR HU values. Ten intensity-modulated radiotherapy/volumetric-modulated arc therapy plans spanning five disease sites (glioma, brain stereotactic radiation therapy (SRT), mediastinal tumor, lung stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT), and prostate cancer) were created on simulation CT for anthropomorphic head, thorax, and pelvis phantoms and recalculated on HyperSight images using the single curve. Validation included ionization-chamber point-dose measurement, 3D gamma analysis, dose-volume histogram comparison, and equivalence testing. Results The averaged 125-kV curve agreed closely with the Philips 120-kV simulation CT curve. All 50 point-dose comparisons fell within ± 2% (82% within ± 1%), with mean differences of -0.24% to + 0.03% across disease sites, kV energies, and reconstruction algorithms. Mean body gamma pass rates were 99.79% (1%/1 mm) and 99.97% (2%/2 mm); mean target pass rates were 98.04% and 99.79%. Target mean-dose differences versus simulation CT averaged 0.11% (maximum 0.46%), and equivalence was confirmed within ± 2%. Conclusions A single, locally generated 125-kV CT-ED/MD curve based on averaged Acuros/MAR HU values enables clinically acceptable HyperSight-based dose calculation, supporting a simplified single-curve commissioning workflow for online adaptive radiotherapy.

All 50 point-dose comparisons fell within ± 2% (82% within ± 1%), with mean differences of -0.24% to + 0.03% across disease sites, kV energies, and reconstruction algorithms. Mean body gamma pass rates were 99.79% (1%/1 mm) and 99.97% (2%/2 mm); mean target pass rates were 98.04% and 99.79%. Target mean-dose differences versus simulation CT averaged 0.11% (maximum 0.46%), and equivalence was confirmed within ± 2%.

Conclusions

A single, locally generated 125-kV CT-ED/MD curve based on averaged Acuros/MAR HU values enables clinically acceptable HyperSight-based dose calculation, supporting a simplified single-curve commissioning workflow for online adaptive radiotherapy.

title: An accessible efficient intervertebral disc vision-language model training strategy with LLM-based retrieval method for spine MRI report generation.
abstract: Background Artificial intelligence (AI) has become increasingly important in healthcare, and multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in understanding and integrating information from medical images and clinical text. This study explores a low-cost and effective MLLM-based approach for automated radiology report generation from lumbar spine MRI, aiming to improve reporting efficiency and consistency. Methods To mitigate the challenges of limited data availability and the high costs associated with applying MLLMs to spinal report generation, we proposed using the axial plane of a single lumbar intervertebral disc (IVD) and the adjacent vertebrae as the research subject. We constructed the pipeline of data processing to get disc-corresponding images and medical reports based on large language models (LLMs). Then, We fine-tuned presently mature MLLMs under conditions of 1125 patient samples and hardware limitations, achieving considerable results. Results In addition to performance evaluated using traditional natural language processing metrics, including BLEU (0.24), ROUGE-L (0.53), and CIDEr (1.28), we further validated the proposed strategy on clinical pathological classification tasks, achieving F1 scores of 0.93 for disc pathology, 0.81 for canal stenosis, and 0.91 for dehydrated disc. Notably, the model achieved diagnostic performance comparable to that of experienced radiologists for canal stenosis and dehydrated disc. These results demonstrate the feasibility of the proposed strategy. Furthermore, our experiments show that the LLM-based data evaluation pipeline is stable and reliable. Conclusion This study offers a new perspective on the field of spinal reporting and outperforms existing methods on both performance and cost. Meanwhile, there is a considerable room for improvement in aspects of data volume and training scale.

title: Diagnostic accuracy of Neuromelanin-sensitive MRI for Parkinson Disease: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
abstract: Introduction Objective: The diagnosis of Parkinson's disease (PD) remains challenging due to clinical overlap with other parkinsonian syndromes and the absence of widely available imaging biomarkers. Neuromelanin-sensitive MRI (NM-MRI) enables in vivo visualization of neuromelanin in the substantia nigra (SN) and locus coeruleus (LC), where signal loss reflects dopaminergic neurodegeneration in the SN and noradrenergic neurodegeneration in the LC. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of NM-MRI in differentiating PD from healthy controls. Materials and methods PubMed, Embase, and the Cochrane Library were searched from inception to February 2025. Studies evaluating the diagnostic accuracy of NM-MRI in PD versus healthy controls were included. Two independent reviewers extracted data and assessed methodological quality using QUADAS-2. Pooled sensitivity and specificity were estimated using a random-effects bivariate model, with construction of a summary receiver operating characteristic (SROC) curve. Subgroup analyses were performed by anatomical region (SN, LC) and imaging parameter (volume, area, signal intensity, contrast ratio, subjective assessment), along with meta-regression and Deeks' funnel plot for publication bias. This review was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251088071). Results Twenty-eight studies comprising 2,268 participants were included. Pooled sensitivity and specificity were 88.0 % (95 % CI, 85.3-90.2 %) and 84.4 % (95 % CI, 80.6-87.5 %), respectively, with an area under the SROC curve of 0.901 and low heterogeneity (I 2 = 3.6 % for sensitivity, 9.2 % for specificity). Volumetric analysis of the SN yielded robust and reproducible performance (sensitivity 88.0 %, specificity 85.5 %), while subjective visual assessment achieved the highest sensitivity (90.8 %) but lower reproducibility. Meta-regression identified no significant effect of MRI acquisition parameters on diagnostic accuracy, and no significant publication bias was detected. Conclusion NM-MRI demonstrates high diagnostic accuracy for differentiating PD from healthy controls, with volumetric analysis of the substantia nigra offering a robust and reproducible imaging biomarker. As the included studies compared PD with healthy controls rather than with other parkinsonian syndromes, these findings should not yet be extrapolated to the differential diagnosis of PD from other forms of parkinsonism.

title: Upper airway morphometry in acute neck infections: Clinical associations and deep learning-based segmentation.
abstract: Objectives Upper airway (UA) compromise is a significant and potentially life-threatening complication of acute neck infection (ANI), but objective, quantitative imaging features are lacking. This study aimed to evaluate the association between UA morphometry in emergency neck MRI and disease severity in ANI, and to develop and evaluate a deep learning (DL)-based model for automatic UA segmentation in ANI patients. Materials and methods A total of 322 patients were included. UA lumen was manually segmented, and prespecified morphometric features were extracted. UA morphometry was correlated with clinical outcomes. Interobserver agreement for all extracted features was evaluated with the Intraclass Correlation Coefficient (ICC). An nnU-Net model was trained on manually segmented data, and its performance was evaluated using the Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC) and feature-specific ICCs. Results ICU admission occurred in 33/322 patients (10.2 %) and prolonged stay (>5 days) in 47/319 (14.7 %). Minimum cross-sectional area, compactness, maximum midline shift, and length of airway narrowing were associated with ICU admission (false-discovery-rate q ≤ 0.008) but not with prolonged stay, and did not significantly improve an established clinical model (AUC 0.80 to 0.84, DeLong p = 0.07 to 0.12). Interobserver agreement was moderate-to-excellent. The nnU-Net reached a median DSC of 0.920 with ICCs of 0.853 to 0.973 and reproduced the ICU associations. Conclusion Quantitative UA morphometry in ANI is reproducible. A narrow caliber, a long narrowed segment, and lateral displacement of the airway are associated with ICU admission, without demonstrated incremental value over established predictors in the prespecified comparison. nnU-Net segmentation reproduces the features and their univariable associations.

title: Diagnostic performance and interobserver agreement of MRI for pancreatic cystic lesions: a multi-reader study with surgical histopathologic correlation.
abstract: Purpose To determine the diagnostic performance and interobserver agreement of MRI for differentiating mucinous from non-mucinous pancreatic cystic lesions (PCLs) and identifying advanced neoplasia using surgical pathology as the reference standard. Methods This retrospective single-center study included surgically resected PCLs with preoperative MRI (2019-2025). Three independent readers blindly assessed cyst subtype and imaging features, including worrisome features (WF) and high-risk stigmata (HRS) according to the 2024 Kyoto guideline. Consensus interpretation was established with a fourth senior abdominal radiologist. Diagnostic performance for mucinous lesion characterization and advanced neoplasia (high-grade dysplasia and invasive carcinoma) was evaluated. Interobserver agreement was assessed using Fleiss κ and Gwet AC1. Logistic regression and ROC analyses identified imaging predictors of advanced neoplasia. Results A total of 85 patients were included (mean age, 66.8 ± 12.5 years; 50.6 % female). At pathology, 70/85 lesions (82.4 %) were mucinous and 23/85 (27.1 %) represented advanced neoplasia, including 21 high-grade dysplasia and two IPMN-derived PDAC. MRI consensus interpretation achieved 100 % sensitivity, 80 % specificity, and 96.5 % accuracy for identifying mucinous lesions. MRI demonstrated 52.2 % sensitivity and 67.7 % specificity for advanced neoplasia using WF or HRS, whereas HRS alone improved specificity (95.2 %) at the expense of sensitivity (21.7 %). All readers correctly identified both cases of IPMN-derived PDAC. Interobserver agreement for cyst subtype classification was fair by Fleiss κ but substantial by Gwet AC1, whereas agreement for detecting advanced neoplasia was moderate. Main pancreatic duct diameter independently predicted advanced neoplasia (OR, 1.18; 95 % CI, 1.01-1.38; p = 0.042) and outperformed cyst size (AUC, 0.69 vs 0.56). Conclusion In this surgically selected cohort, consensus MRI differentiates mucinous from nonmucinous PCLs with high sensitivity. Detection of advanced neoplasia, particularly noninvasive high-grade dysplasia, remains challenging because of overlap with low-grade lesions. Fair-to-moderate interobserver agreement highlights the challenges of MRI-based risk stratification. The surgically selected cohort provides histopathologic confirmation but should be considered when interpreting performance estimates in the broader surveillance population.

title: Virtual low-keV CT imaging enhances tumor contrast and provides favorable diagnostic assessability in oral cavity carcinoma: Comparison with MRI and polyenergetic CT.
abstract: Background Low-energy virtual monoenergetic imaging (VMI) improves tumor contrast in contrast-enhanced CT. Whether it can provide tumor delineation comparable to MRI in oral cavity carcinoma remains unclear. Objective To compare objective and subjective image quality, artifact burden, and two-dimensional tumor area measurements between 40-keV VMI, conventional polyenergetic CT images (PEI), and contrast-enhanced MRI in patients with oral cavity carcinoma. Methods Seventy-two patients (33 women; mean age, 70.2 ± 11.9 years) with newly diagnosed oral cavity carcinoma underwent contrast-enhanced MRI and dual-source dual-energy CT. Forty-keV VMI, PEI, and contrast-enhanced T1-weighted MRI with Dixon-based fat saturation were compared. Objective image quality was assessed using ROI-based measurements of tumor attenuation and contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR). Three readers independently noted 2D tumor dimensions and rated metal and motion artifacts as well as diagnostic assessability. Results Tumor attenuation was significantly higher in VMI than in PEI (median, 274.3 [IQR 236.7-316.5] vs 136.3 [114.9-154.5] HU), as was CNR (10.4 [6.6-15.8] vs 7.6 [3.3-11.9]; both p < 0.001). In five patients, severe metal artifacts rendered CT non-diagnostic. Among the 67 patients with evaluable examinations across all three modalities, median tumor area was 285.0 mm 2 (IQR 195.0-705.0) in VMI, 320.0 mm 2 (IQR 206.0-701.0) in PEI, and 312.0 mm 2 (IQR 210.0-692.0) in MRI. The overall comparison was significant (p = 0.021), but no pairwise differences remained significant after correction for multiple comparisons. Metal artifacts were more pronounced in VMI than MRI (p < 0.001), whereas motion artifacts were more common in MRI (p < 0.001). Overall diagnostic assessability was higher for VMI and MRI than for PEI (both p ≤ 0.009). Inter-reader agreement was moderate to excellent (ICC ≥ 0.72). Conclusion Low-energy VMI improves objective tumor attenuation and contrast-to-noise ratio compared with conventional PEI. Subjective diagnostic assessability ratings were favorable for both VMI and MRI, whereas metal artifacts were more pronounced in VMI and motion artifacts were more common in MRI. Although no pairwise differences in tumor area remained statistically significant after correction for multiple comparisons, these findings do not establish equivalence in tumor delineation or diagnostic performance compared with MRI.

title: Prognostic value of native T1 mapping and extracellular volume fraction in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
abstract: Background Accurate risk stratification in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) remains challenging, and the prognostic significance of cardiovascular magnetic resonance-derived native T1 mapping and extracellular volume fraction (ECV) remains uncertain. Aims To systematically evaluate the prognostic value of native T1 mapping and ECV in HCM patients. Methods PubMed, Embase, MEDLINE, and the Cochrane Library were searched from inception to February 6, 2026. Eligible studies assessed native T1 and/or ECV for prognosis in HCM. Baseline values, mean differences, and hazard ratios (HRs) were synthesized using random-effects models. Effect estimates were standardized as HRs per 30-ms increase in native T1 and per 1% increase in ECV. Results Eight longitudinal cohort studies involving 2539 HCM patients were included. Elevated native T1 was significantly associated with an increased risk of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) (HR=1.27, 95% CI: 1.12-1.44, P < 0.001), as was higher ECV (HR=1.10, 95% CI: 1.07-1.14, P < 0.001). For sudden cardiac death-related outcomes, the association with native T1 was not significant, whereas elevated ECV was associated with an increased risk (HR=1.14, 95% CI: 1.01-1.28, P = 0.04), although substantial heterogeneity was observed and sensitivity analysis indicated limited robustness (HR=1.05, 95% CI: 0.97-1.14, P = 0.21). For heart failure-related outcomes, only ECV was associated with risk (HR=1.10, 95% CI: 1.05-1.15; P < 0.001). Conclusions Native T1 and ECV were associated with MACE risk in HCM, and ECV was additionally associated with heart failure-related outcomes. Their value for sudden cardiac death-related risk prediction requires further validation. Prospero registration number CRD420261406609.

title: Multicentre assessment of interactive 3D holograms for enhanced preoperative planning for colorectal liver metastasis resection.
abstract: Surgical planning for colorectal liver metastasis (CRLM) is crucial for achieving curative resection. The advent of artificial intelligence and automatic image segmentation has made 3D holograms readily available for surgical planning. Conventional patient imaging can now be converted into interactive 3D models and displayed in augmented reality (AR). This multicentre, observational study evaluated the impact of 3D visualisation on surgical planning for CRLM. 46 surgeons from 21 liver surgery centres in nine countries assessed eight complex CRLM cases. Each case included CT portal venous phase images and a 3D hologram displayed in AR, created using an automatic segmentation tool and quality assessed by radiologists. Surgeons completed four surveys covering experience, initial CT-based management, post-3D review management, and perceived benefit. Among the participants (33 consultants, 13 residents), 24% worked in centres performing 50-100 resections per year, and 70% in centres performing over 100 per year. The 3D holograms changed resectability assessments in 20% of cases (8% from inoperable to operable; 12% from operable to inoperable). Management decisions between neoadjuvant therapy and surgery changed in 21% of cases, and 22% of surgeons modified their surgical approach. Most surgeons (96%) found the technology easy to use, valuing it for complex cases (61%), tumour board discussions (83%), and teaching (98%). 3D holographic imaging can influence CRLM management decisions. The technology is acceptable to liver surgeons with multiple potential clinical applications. Prospective, randomised studies are needed to evaluate its clinical implementation and impact on patient outcomes.

title: Prognosis of Patients with Delayed Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm Rupture after Endovascular Aortic Repair: A Multicentre Retrospective Study in France.
abstract: Objective The majority of patients with abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) undergo endovascular aortic repair (EVAR). Despite its high overall success rate, EVAR does not eliminate the risk of aneurysm rupture. This study aimed to evaluate the prognosis of patients undergoing surgical management for post-EVAR rupture. Methods A multicentre retrospective study of patients who presented with ruptured AAA after successful EVAR between 2007 and 2022 at 22 academic hospitals was conducted. The index EVAR procedures were performed between 2002 and 2020. Data were extracted from electronic hospital records and computed tomography scans. Death during follow up was ascertained using the French register of deceased persons. Survival probabilities at 30, 90, and 365 days were estimated with Kaplan-Meier estimators. Cox proportional hazards survival regression was used to identify determinants associated with increased risk of death. Results One hundred and nine patients (96 men) were included, with a mean age of 79.1 ± 9 years at the time of rupture. The median time from index EVAR to rupture was 50 months (range 0 - 179 months). Sixty-seven patients had open surgery (of which 37% underwent suprarenal cross clamping), 39 received endovascular treatment, and three underwent hybrid repair. Overall mortality was 26.6% at thirty days, increasing to 33.9% at ninety days, and 41.3% at 1 year. Neither the type of endoleak nor the type of repair was significantly associated with risk of death during follow up. Post-operative complications were frequent, including renal complications (44.0%), major haemorrhage (22.9%), respiratory distress (19.3%), and mesenteric ischaemia (6%). Conclusion This study presented a large multicentre series of patients treated for ruptured AAA after EVAR. Despite considerable progress in stent graft technology, EVAR offers little protection in the event of late rupture, even among patients with type II endoleak only. The mortality rate in this study is within the range of those published based on de novo AAA rupture.

title: Morphometric MRI analysis of the isthmus tonsillaris in patients with crossbite.
abstract: Background To characterize the minimum cross-sectional area of the isthmus tonsillaris using standardized magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and investigate its association with crossbite. Methods This retrospective observational study included standardized MRI examinations performed between 2002 and 2008. Thirty-six untreated subjects fulfilled the predefined inclusion criteria, comprising 26 patients with anterior and/or posterior crossbite and 10 controls with normal transverse occlusion. The minimum cross-sectional area of the isthmus tonsillaris was measured using a standardized morphometric MRI protocol. Group comparisons were performed using the Mann-Whitney U test. Exploratory analyses investigated associations with age and transverse discrepancy. Results The mean minimum cross-sectional area measured 42.29 mm² in the crossbite group and 139.9 mm² in controls. No overlap was observed: the highest value in the crossbite group (80.5 mm²) remained below the lowest value in controls (87.0 mm²) (P < 0.001). No relevant differences were identified between sexes or crossbite subtypes. No linear association was found between negative transverse discrepancy and the minimum cross-sectional area. Exploratory analysis suggested an age-related increase in the minimum cross-sectional area in subjects with normal transverse occlusion, whereas this developmental pattern was not observed in patients with crossbite. Conclusions Patients with anterior and/or posterior crossbite demonstrated a reduced minimum cross-sectional area of the isthmus tonsillaris compared with subjects with normal transverse occlusion. These findings identify the isthmus tonsillaris as a relevant anatomical region warranting investigation in orthodontic diagnosis and interdisciplinary airway research. Future cone-beam computed tomography studies may provide datasets to validate these findings while adhering to the ALARA principle.

title: Impact of BRCA2, BRCA1, and Other Individual Homologous Recombination Repair Alterations on Survival in Metastatic Castration-resistant Prostate Cancer.
abstract: Background and objective The clinical significance of homologous recombination repair (HRR) alterations beyond BRCA2 in advanced prostate cancer is poorly understood. We investigated the association of individual non-BRCA2 HRR alterations with outcomes of patients treated with first-line therapy for metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer. Methods Eligible patients from the prospective CAPTURE study underwent somatic/germ line DNA analyses using a next-generation sequencing panel including ATM, BRCA1, BRCA2, BRIP1, CDK12, CHEK2, FANCA, HDAC2, PALB2, RAD51B, and RAD54L. Association with overall survival (OS) and radiographic progression-free survival was assessed using multivariable Cox regression models comparing individual non-BRCA2 HRR alterations to those in patients with BRCA2 alterations or without HRR alterations. Key findings and limitations A total of 1010 patients were included, with BRCA2 and non-BRCA2 HRR alterations found in 122 (12%) and 191 (19%) patients, respectively. BRCA1, ATM, FANCA, HDAC2, CHEK2, CDK12, and BRIP1 alterations were observed in 19 (1.9%), 69 (6.8%), 34 (3.4%), 24 (2.4%), 23 (2.3%), 20 (2%), and 15 (1.5%) patients, respectively. Patients with ATM (hazard ratio [HR] 1.66; 95% confidence interval [CI] = 1.20-2.30; p = 0.002) or CHEK2 (HR 1.71; 95% CI = 1.03-2.90; p = 0.039) alterations showed improved OS compared to patients with BRCA2 alterations, with similar outcomes to patients without HRR alterations. BRCA1 (HR 0.49; 95% CI = 0.30-0.80; p = 0.004), FANCA (HR 0.61; 95% CI = 0.42-0.89; p = 0.011), and CDK12 (HR 0.57; 95% CI = 0.35-0.93; p = 0.025) were associated with worse OS compared to patients without HRR alterations, with similar outcomes to patients with BRCA2 alterations. Conclusions and clinical implications Prognostic associations differ across individual HRR alterations. Although BRCA1, FANCA, or HDAC mutations were associated with a prognosis similar to that associated with BRCA2 alterations, prognosis in patients with ATM or CHEK2 alterations was similar to that in patients without HRR alterations. In the research setting, non-BRCA2 HRR alterations should be analyzed and reported as individual entities whenever possible.

In the research setting, non-BRCA2 HRR alterations should be analyzed and reported as individual entities whenever possible.

title: An OCT-based Structural Evaluation Framework for Laser-Induced Retinal Lesions in Mice and Exploratory Application Under ALDH2 Modulation.
abstract: Laser-induced retinal injury models require structural assessments that capture lesion heterogeneity. We developed a five-dimensional optical coherence tomography (OCT) framework and explored its application under aldehyde dehydrogenase 2 (ALDH2) modulation. Following 532-nm left-eye photocoagulation, mice received dimethyl sulfoxide vehicle, Alda-1, or Daidzin intraperitoneally for seven days. OCT, fundus photography, and fluorescein angiography were performed 24 h after the final dose. The framework integrated morphologic classification, five-domain severity scoring, lesion geometry, layer-specific thickness and normalized area under the thickness-distance curve (AUC), and anatomically matched contralateral comparisons. Thirty-six lesions from nine mice were analyzed. Classification and scoring showed high interobserver agreement (κ = 0.839; intraclass correlation coefficient = 0.925). After Benjamini-Hochberg adjustment, severity score was the only tested outcome differing significantly among subtypes; eight of 45 structural correlations were significant. In 32 matched pairs, all six thickness comparisons showed significantly lower lesion-eye values. Correlations between local thickness and normalized AUC were significant after contralateral subtraction for outer retinal and outer nuclear layer measurements at the lesion level, whereas absolute correlations were nonsignificant; only the former remained significant at the mouse level. Alda-1 and Daidzin differed in subtype composition. Mouse-clustered models indicated lower scores, greater outer nuclear layer first-point thickness, and larger margin angles with Alda-1, but mouse-level comparisons were nonsignificant. Normalized AUC and its contralateral differences showed no significant treatment differences at either level. This framework integrates qualitative, semiquantitative, and quantitative assessments to characterize OCT-visible structural features in mouse retinal laser injury models.

title: Ring-based OCT protocol for retinal ganglion cell complex thickness analysis in mice.
abstract: Optical coherence tomography (OCT) enables non-invasive, high-resolution imaging of retinal layers and is widely used to assess structural changes in preclinical models of retinal and optic nerve disease. However, OCT-based retinal thickness measurements in rodents remain insufficiently standardized, with differences in measurement location and segmentation methodology potentially limiting reproducibility and comparability across studies. We describe a standardized OCT-based protocol for ganglion cell complex (GCC) thickness measurement in mice using predefined retinal landmarks and manual segmentation. Six radial OCT scans separated by 30° are acquired around the optic nerve head, and GCC thickness is measured using ImageJ at three nominal radial distances on each side of the optic nerve: 1000, 1500, and 2000 μm. The applicability of the protocol was evaluated in a murine optic nerve crush (ONC) model. GCC thickness decreased significantly over time, from 68.8 ± 5.2 μm at baseline to 60.7 ± 8.0 μm at day 15 and 60.6 ± 9.8 μm at day 24. Radius- and quadrant-specific analyses further demonstrated the ability of the protocol to detect regional patterns of GCC thinning. This protocol provides a structured approach for OCT-based GCC thickness assessment in mice and may improve consistency and comparability across preclinical studies.

title: Adiposity measures in relation to cognitive screening performance and MRI-derived brain age gap in middle-aged and older adults.
abstract: Background Adiposity has pernicious health implications, notably contributing to cognitive decline and neuroanatomical alterations. Research regarding which measures of adiposity are most related to cognition and the brain is inconsistent. This study explores the relationships between 1) multiple adiposity measures, 2) adiposity measures and cognitive screening performance, and 3) adiposity measures and a machine-learning predicted brain age gap (BAG). Methods Cross-sectional data were combined from two multi-site studies, including 641 non-Hispanic black and non-Hispanic white adults (45-85 years old). Adiposity measures included Body Mass Index (BMI), waist circumference (WC), waist-to-hip ratio (WHpR), waist-to-height ratio (WHtR), and A Body Shape Index (ABSI) z-score. Cognition was assessed using the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) and Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA). MoCA scores were converted to equivalent MMSE scores. The predicted BAG was obtained using DeepBrainNet (n = 204) from T1-weighted brain MRI. Results Adiposity measures were significantly correlated, except for BMI and ABSI. After covariate adjustment, cognitive screening associations were small and inconsistent, with a linear association for BMI and nonlinear associations for WC and WHtR. BAG associations depended on model form, with nonlinear patterns for BMI, WC, and WHtR and higher predicted BAG at higher versus intermediate adiposity levels. Combining adiposity measures showed little additional predictive value. Conclusions Anthropometric adiposity measures, particularly BMI, WC, and WHtR, were more consistently related to MRI-derived brain age gap than to brief cognitive screening performance in a cohort of middle-aged and older adults. These findings describe cross-sectional associations with older predicted brain age, especially at higher adiposity levels.

title: French AFU Cancer Committee Guidelines - Update 2026-2028: Upper urinary tract urothelial tumors (UTUC).
abstract: Introduction The purpose of this article is to propose an update of the French guidelines from the national committee ccAFU on upper tract urothelial carcinomas (UTUC). Methods A systematic Medline search for epidemiology, risk factors, diagnosis, prognosis, treatment options and follow-up of UTUC was performed between 2024 and 2026 to evaluate the available references and their levels of evidence. Results UTUC is a rare malignancy with specific risk factors, including exposure to aristolochic acid and Lynch syndrome. Its diagnosis is based on the use of computed tomography urography and ureterorenoscopy with biopsies. A prognostic classification has been proposed to discriminate low- and high-risk lesions mainly on the basis of tumor grade (low/high) and imaging aspect (noninfiltrative/infiltrative). Tumor size (<2/≥2cm), focality (uni/multifocal), and hydronephrosis (absent/present) are more relative risk factors. The standard of care for low-risk patients is currently conservative treatment involving mainly ureterorenoscopy laser ablation, whereas radical nephroureterectomy (RNU) is advised for those with high-risk disease. Adjuvant treatments after RNU include the intravesical instillation of chemotherapy to decrease the risk of bladder recurrence and the delivery of platinum-based chemotherapy in pT2-T4 and/or pN+ patients. First-line treatment for metastatic UTUC is based on the use of a combination of enfortumab vedotin plus pembrolizumab. For unfit patients, platinum-based chemotherapy plus nivolumab followed by maintenance nivolumab in those with at least stable disease or platinum-based chemotherapy followed by maintenance avelumab in those with at least stable disease can be proposed. The surveillance regimen and schedule depend on the disease stage. Conclusion These updated guidelines will contribute to improving the management of patients diagnosed with UTUC.

title: French AFU Cancer Committee Guidelines - Update 2026-2028: Kidney cancer.
abstract: Objective To update recommendations for the management of kidney cancer. Methods A systematic review of the literature published between 2014 and 2026 was performed to identify relevant evidence on diagnosis, classification, treatment, and follow-up. Recommendations were graded as strong or weak. Results Contrast-enhanced thoraco-abdominal CT remains the reference for diagnosis and staging, while PET/CT is not routinely indicated. Percutaneous biopsy is recommended when it may influence therapeutic decision-making and reduce unnecessary surgery for benign tumors. Tumors are classified according to the 2017 pTNM classification (revised in 2025), the 2022 WHO classification, and ISUP grade; metastatic disease is stratified by IMDC risk group. For T1 tumors, minimally invasive robot-assisted partial nephrectomy is the reference surgical treatment. Active surveillance should be offered for masses≤2cm regardless of age and may be considered for selected tumors up to 4cm. Ablative therapies and stereotactic radiotherapy are alternatives for patients unsuitable for surgery. Radical nephrectomy remains the standard for locally advanced disease, and adjuvant pembrolizumab is recommended for patients at high risk of recurrence. Immediate cytoreductive nephrectomy is not recommended in poor-risk metastatic disease. First-line treatment of metastatic clear cell RCC relies on immune checkpoint inhibitor-based combinations according to IMDC risk. Clinical trial enrollment should be prioritized after progression on adjuvant pembrolizumab and in later treatment lines. Patients with non-clear cell RCC should undergo expert multidisciplinary review, with priority given to clinical trials. Appropriate use of healthcare resources and environmental sustainability are integrated throughout the recommendations. Conclusions These updated recommendations incorporate recent advances in diagnosis, surgery, systemic therapy, and disease monitoring, providing a contemporary evidence-based framework for the management of kidney cancer across disease stages.

Active surveillance should be offered for masses≤2cm regardless of age and may be considered for selected tumors up to 4cm. Ablative therapies and stereotactic radiotherapy are alternatives for patients unsuitable for surgery. Radical nephrectomy remains the standard for locally advanced disease, and adjuvant pembrolizumab is recommended for patients at high risk of recurrence. Immediate cytoreductive nephrectomy is not recommended in poor-risk metastatic disease. First-line treatment of metastatic clear cell RCC relies on immune checkpoint inhibitor-based combinations according to IMDC risk. Clinical trial enrollment should be prioritized after progression on adjuvant pembrolizumab and in later treatment lines. Patients with non-clear cell RCC should undergo expert multidisciplinary review, with priority given to clinical trials. Appropriate use of healthcare resources and environmental sustainability are integrated throughout the recommendations.

Conclusions

These updated recommendations incorporate recent advances in diagnosis, surgery, systemic therapy, and disease monitoring, providing a contemporary evidence-based framework for the management of kidney cancer across disease stages.

title: French AFU Cancer Committee Guidelines - Update 2026-2028: Muscle-invasive bladder tumors (MIBC).
abstract: Objective To update the CCAFU guidelines for the management of muscle-invasive bladder cancer (MIBC). Methods A systematic review (Medline) of the literature from 2024 to 2026 was performed, considering the diagnostic work-up, treatment options, and NMIBC and MIBC follow-up, with references graded according to their level of evidence. Results The diagnosis of muscle-invasive bladder cancer relies on transurethral resection of the bladder. The staging work-up includes CT urography combined with chest CT. Multiparametric bladder MRI may be proposed to refine locoregional assessment without delaying management. For nonmetastatic disease, radical cystectomy with standard pelvic lymph node dissection remains the reference treatment. In cisplatin-eligible patients, a perioperative strategy based on cisplatin-based neoadjuvant chemotherapy should be discussed, with consideration of integrating immunotherapy and perioperative systemic treatment according to available indications. The combination of enfortumab vedotin and pembrolizumab (EVP) is also recommended. In cisplatin-ineligible patients, EVP represents a major therapeutic option when available. A bladder-sparing strategy using trimodal therapy-combining maximal transurethral resection, external beam radiotherapy, and concomitant radiosensitizing chemotherapy-should be discussed and offered to selected, well-informed patients who are compliant with rigorous follow-up. Urinary diversion by enterocystoplasty may be offered to both men and women in the absence of oncologic, functional, or general contraindications; otherwise, ileal conduit urinary diversion remains the reference diversion. Enrollment in an enhanced recovery program after surgery is recommended for all surgical patients. For metastatic disease, the EVP combination is the recommended first-line treatment. After disease progression, subsequent therapeutic options should be tailored according to previously received treatments, patient profiles, potential molecular alterations, and access to clinical trials. Conclusion This update of the CCAFU guidelines aims to harmonize and optimize the management of patients with muscle-invasive bladder cancer, incorporating recent developments in diagnostic work-up, perioperative treatments, bladder-preservation strategies, and the management of metastatic disease.

title: French AFU Cancer Committee Guidelines - Update 2026-2028: Penile cancer.
abstract: Objective To update the French guidelines of the Cancer Committee of the French Association of Urology on the epidemiology, prevention, diagnosis, treatment, and follow-up of penile tumors for the 2026-2028 period. Materials and methods A comprehensive review of the literature published since the previous update, up to 2026, was performed. Recent international classifications and guidelines were incorporated. The available literature was assessed according to its level of evidence to formulate recommendations applicable to clinical practice. Results Squamous cell carcinomas account for 95% of invasive penile cancers. Two carcinogenic pathways are recognized, HPV dependent and HPV independent, the latter being notably associated with lichen sclerosus and chronic inflammation. Prevention is based on HPV vaccination, patient information regarding risk factors, and the management of chronic inflammatory conditions. Any persistent penile lesion should prompt biopsy without delay. Clinical examination remains essential for local staging and may be supplemented by magnetic resonance imaging when an organ-preserving strategy is considered. Treatment should favor organ preservation whenever oncologically feasible, with negative surgical margins being mandatory. Lymph node assessment is a major prognostic determinant. In clinically node-negative patients with intermediate- or high-risk tumors, bilateral sentinel lymph node biopsy is recommended. In clinically node-positive patients, 18-FDG PET contributes to staging, although histological confirmation remains necessary. Radical inguinal lymph node dissection is indicated in patients with proven nodal involvement. For cN3 disease, neoadjuvant chemotherapy is recommended, followed by surgery in responders. In the metastatic setting, chemotherapy remains the standard treatment. Data concerning immunotherapy are encouraging but remain insufficient to support its use outside clinical trials. Intensive follow-up should be performed during the first 2 years and should include local and inguinal examinations, patient self-examination, quality-of-life assessments, and psychosexual support. Conclusion The management of penile cancer relies on early diagnosis, organ preservation whenever feasible, and prompt risk-adapted lymph node management. Centralization of care within expert multidisciplinary teams is essential for optimizing oncological, functional, and psychosexual outcomes.

title: French AFU Cancer Committee Guidelines - Update 2026-2028: Testicular germ cell cancer.
abstract: Objective To update the guidelines for the management of testicular germ cell tumors. Materials and methods A comprehensive literature review in PubMed was conducted for articles published from 2024 through July 2026 that addressed the diagnosis, treatment, follow-up, and treatment-related toxicity of testicular germ cell tumors (TGCTs). The level of evidence of the selected articles was assessed. Results The initial evaluation of a patient with a testicular germ cell tumor is based on clinical examination, serum tumor marker assessment including Alpha-foetoprotein (AFP), total human Chorionic Gonadotrophin (hCG), and lactate deshydrogenase (LDH) levels, and imaging, including scrotal ultrasonography and contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis. Radical inguinal orchiectomy is the first therapeutic step. It provides the histologic diagnosis, establishes the local stage, and identifies prognostic risk factors in patients with stage I nonseminomatous germ cell tumors (NSGCTs). In patients with stage I pure seminoma, the risk of relapse is 15-20%; active surveillance is therefore preferred in compliant patients. Adjuvant chemotherapy with one cycle of carboplatin at an area under the curve of 7 is an option, whereas indications for lombo-aortic radiotherapy are limited. For patients with stage I NSGCT, a risk-adapted strategy - active surveillance or one cycle of BEP chemotherapy (bleomycin, etoposide, and cisplatin), according to the absence or presence of lymphovascular invasion - is preferred over universal surveillance. Staging based on retroperitoneal lymph node dissection has a limited role. Metastatic TGCTs are most commonly treated with BEP chemotherapy, provided that bleomycin is not contraindicated. The number of cycles is determined according to the International Germ Cell Cancer Collaborative Group prognostic classification. Lombo-aortic radiotherapy and chemotherapy are both standard options for stage IIA seminomatous germ cell tumors (SGCTs) and selected low-volume stage IIB tumors. Treatment de-escalation protocols may be considered at expert centers for selected patients with metastatic stage IIA SGCT. Nerve-sparing retroperitoneal lymph node dissection at an expert center may be offered to patients with marker-negative stage IIA NSGCTs. When chemotherapy is indicated, the residual mass size must be assessed at the end of treatment by CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis in patients with NSGCTs. The resection of residual masses is recommended for any residual NSGCT mass larger than 1cm. In patients with SGCTs, reassessment with 18 F-FDG PET is recommended for residual masses larger than 3cm to guide the indication for surgery. Surgery remains uncommon in these settings. Guideline-based follow-up should be offered to all patients, together with education on testicular self-examination. Conclusions Adherence to TGCT management guidelines results in excellent cancer-specific survival rates of 99% for patients with stage I disease and more than 85% for patients with metastatic disease.

For patients with stage I NSGCT, a risk-adapted strategy - active surveillance or one cycle of BEP chemotherapy (bleomycin, etoposide, and cisplatin), according to the absence or presence of lymphovascular invasion - is preferred over universal surveillance. Staging based on retroperitoneal lymph node dissection has a limited role. Metastatic TGCTs are most commonly treated with BEP chemotherapy, provided that bleomycin is not contraindicated. The number of cycles is determined according to the International Germ Cell Cancer Collaborative Group prognostic classification. Lombo-aortic radiotherapy and chemotherapy are both standard options for stage IIA seminomatous germ cell tumors (SGCTs) and selected low-volume stage IIB tumors. Treatment de-escalation protocols may be considered at expert centers for selected patients with metastatic stage IIA SGCT. Nerve-sparing retroperitoneal lymph node dissection at an expert center may be offered to patients with marker-negative stage IIA NSGCTs. When chemotherapy is indicated, the residual mass size must be assessed at the end of treatment by CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis in patients with NSGCTs. The resection of residual masses is recommended for any residual NSGCT mass larger than 1cm. In patients with SGCTs, reassessment with 18F-FDG PET is recommended for residual masses larger than 3cm to guide the indication for surgery. Surgery remains uncommon in these settings. Guideline-based follow-up should be offered to all patients, together with education on testicular self-examination.

Conclusions

Adherence to TGCT management guidelines results in excellent cancer-specific survival rates of 99% for patients with stage I disease and more than 85% for patients with metastatic disease.

title: PSMA PET Before Prostate Biopsy: From Lesion Detection to Biopsy Avoidance.
abstract: Introduction Prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA) positron emission tomography (PET) may refine biopsy selection when magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is equivocal or nonsuspicious despite persistent clinical concern. This review aims to examine the prospective evidence and to distinguish diagnostic accuracy from biopsy avoidance. Methods Selected prospective cohorts and randomized trials evaluating PSMA PET before prostate biopsy were synthesized narratively, alongside relevant systematic reviews and guidelines. Interpretation focused on patient selection, clinically significant prostate cancer (csPCa) definitions, biopsy protocols, and verification of PET-negative findings. Results Combining PSMA PET with MRI improves sensitivity and negative predictive value in several prospective studies, particularly in men with equivocal findings. PET-targeted biopsy can improve sampling, but this does not establish the safety of omitting biopsy. In PRIMARY2, a PET-guided pathway achieved noninferior csPCa detection compared with systematic biopsy (12% versus 16%; prespecified noninferiority margin, 10 percentage points), while 49% of men in the PET arm avoided biopsy within 6 months. PET-negative men did not undergo routine immediate biopsy, so the trial does not establish histologically verified negative predictive value. Study heterogeneity and limited follow-up constrain generalization. Conclusions PSMA PET may complement MRI in selected men with residual diagnostic uncertainty. Broader implementation requires validated clinical thresholds, longer follow-up after biopsy deferral, and evidence of cost-effectiveness.

title: Three-dimensional deep-learning age estimation from the fourth rib on high-resolution CT: An evaluative likelihood-ratio approach.
abstract: For four decades, age estimation from the fourth rib has rested on İşcan's visual phase system, which requires the physical bone and returns an ordinal category, not a calibrated probability. We developed a three-dimensional deep-learning pipeline, automated downstream of AI-assisted segmentation, that estimates age from the whole rib on computed tomography (CT) and reports a likelihood ratio. Right fourth ribs from thin-section (1 mm) chest CT of 453 living adults (225 men, 228 women; 18.0-99.8 years) were segmented, posed canonically and encoded as four representations: metric multi-view RGB-D renderings and a point cloud of the sternal end, a point cloud of the complete rib, and twenty morphometric scalars. Sex-specific networks trained by label-distribution learning were evaluated on a frozen hold-out set (three seeds). The selected estimators reached a mean absolute error of 10.6 years in men and 10.4 in women (45-46% below a mean-age predictor; 9.0 and 8.4 years between ages 18 and 70). Likelihood ratios were informative at every threshold from 30 to 70 years (Cllr < 1), sex was classified with an area under the ROC curve of 0.966, and intra-observer reproducibility was ICC 0.872, limited chiefly by the canonical pose. The age signal was not confined to the sternal extremity examined by phase scoring: in women the complete rib outperformed the sternal end (10.4 versus 14.6 years); in men the two were equivalent, consistent with sex-specific standards. Because 1 mm sections cannot resolve İşcan's fine relief, higher-resolution surface capture is a priority for future work.

title: An Anatomical Study of the Middle Hepatic Vein in Close Proximity to the Cystic Plate and Its Underappreciated Clinical Significance in Laparoscopic Hepatectomy (with Video).
abstract: Background and purpose The middle hepatic vein (MHV) is a key landmark for anatomical liver resection, but its peripheral relationship to the cystic plate has mainly been considered a bleeding hazard during cholecystectomy. We examined this relationship and its potential utility as an early landmark during caudal-approach laparoscopic hepatectomy. Materials and methods Fifty-six patients undergoing laparoscopic liver resection involving the main portal fissure between August 2020 and September 2022 were retrospectively reviewed. The shortest distance between the MHV or its nearest branch and the cystic plate was assessed using preoperative CT and three-dimensional reconstruction and categorized as ≤1mm or >1mm. Two hepatobiliary surgeons independently reviewed the imaging findings. In patients with a branch within 1mm, intraoperative identification and tracing to the main MHV were assessed. Results The closest MHV branch was within 1mm of the cystic plate in 12 patients (21%) and >1mm in 44 (79%). Interobserver classification agreed in 55 of 56 patients (98.2%; Cohen's κ=0.95). In all 12 patients with a branch within 1mm, the corresponding branch was identified at the anticipated intraoperative location without injury and successfully traced to the main MHV. Conclusions An MHV branch lies immediately beneath the cystic plate in approximately one-fifth of patients. When identified preoperatively, it may represent both a vascular structure at risk of injury and a potential anatomical starting point for tracing the main MHV during a caudal approach. Comparative studies are needed to determine its effect on operative efficiency or safety.

title: [Place of clinical breast examination in breast cancer screening strategies. French College of Gynecologists and Obstetricians (CNGOF) recommendations for clinical practice].
abstract: France, like many countries around the world, is facing a rise in the incidence of breast cancer. Numerous studies have shown that the risk of death is linked to the initial stage of the tumor. In this context, mammographic screening for breast cancer aims to diagnose cancers at a subclinical stage, to limit treatment-related morbidity and reduce mortality. In France, this screening is recommended every two years for women aged 50 to 74, while clinical breast examination (CBE) by a healthcare professional is recommended by the Haute Autorité de Santé (HAS) starting at age 25, to be performed annually with no upper age limit. However, the practice of CBE needs to be updated, particularly regarding its impact on the number of cancers diagnosed, their stage, and mortality, considering new data from international literature. Design The GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) method was used to assess the quality of the evidence on which these recommendations were based. Methods The Senology Commission (SC) of the French College of Gynecologists and Obstetricians examined 16 questions regarding CBE, distinguishing four groups of women (the general population with or without mammography screening, women over 70 years of age, high or very-risk women, and women previously treated for breast cancer). For each scenario, it was determined whether performing a CBE, compared with not performing it, led to the detection of more breast cancers, reduced tumor size, or improved survival. One question addressed the training requirements for CBE. Results The SC issued three recommendations aimed at: 1) recommending annual CBE for women in the general population aged 30 to 74, 2) recommending annual CBE for women who have previously been treated for breast cancer, 3) recommending that CBE be performed by a trained healthcare professional. The SC issued four position statements aimed at: 1) not advising CBE for women in the general population under the age of 30, as the procedure carries a risk of unnecessary follow-up tests in a group of women where the incidence of breast cancer is very low. 2) advising performing a CBE during breast cancer screening; 3) advising an annual CBE for women over 75 years of age, with the discontinuation of this practice depending on comorbidities and life expectancy. 4) advising annual CBE for women at high and very high-risk starting at age 20. According to the experts of the CNGOF's Scientific Committee, a CBE should be performed only after obtaining explicit consent following the provision of information on its benefits and risks. The SC urges all women who notice a change or abnormality in their breasts to consult their doctor without delay to undergo a clinical breast exam.
