title: Multimodal multitask deep learning for predicting tertiary lymphoid structures and peritoneal recurrence in gastric cancer: a multicentre development, validation, and testing study.
abstract: Peritoneal recurrence remains a common and fatal complication following curative gastric cancer surgery. Tertiary lymphoid structures are crucial indicators of immune response in cancer, and their maturation is associated with better prognosis and therapy outcomes. Evaluation of these structures could improve patient stratification for treatment of cancer but is hindered by the invasive and biased nature of histological methods. This study aimed to explore a non-invasive radiological method of assessment in patients with gastric cancer, using a novel multitask hybrid model to predict the presence and maturation status of tertiary lymphoid structures and peritoneal recurrence-free survival. We developed CTransNet, a multitask hybrid model combining a convolutional neural network (ResNet50) and a Transformer model to predict tertiary lymphoid structure maturation and peritoneal recurrence-free survival in patients with gastric cancer. The study used retrospective data from eight Chinese cohorts of patients treated for gastric cancer at Nanfang Hospital, Sun Yat-sen University Cancer Center, Yunnan Cancer Hospital, and Guangdong Provincial Hospital of Chinese Medicine (one training cohort, two internal validation cohorts, three external validation cohorts, and two independent cohorts of patients treated with anti-PD-1 or anti-PD-L1 inhibitors for at least two cycles). Patients were classified into three categories based on the presence and maturation of tertiary lymphoid structures (identified using haematoxylin-eosin and immunohistochemistry staining): TLS0 (absent tertiary lymphoid structures), TLS1 (primary follicle-like tertiary lymphoid structures without germinal centres), and TLS2 (secondary follicle-like tertiary lymphoid structures with germinal centres [ie, more mature structures]). Peritoneal recurrence was assessed using imaging (ultrasonography, CT, or PET-CT), clinical signs, or reoperation. We evaluated the accuracy of the multitask hybrid model in classifying patient-level tertiary lymphoid structure status using receiver operating characteristic analysis. Patients were stratified into risk groups using the median predicted score from the training cohort (high vs low), which was then applied to the validation cohorts. Survival outcomes (peritoneal recurrence-free survival, disease-free survival, and overall survival) were analysed using Kaplan-Meier methods and Cox proportional hazards models. We also analysed the relationships between predicted scores and responses to chemotherapy and immunotherapy. Patients in the Chinese cohorts were recruited between Jan 1, 2005, and Feb 28, 2022. In the training cohort, for classifying patient-level tertiary lymphoid structure status, values for area under the receiver operating characteristic curve were 0·910 (95% CI 0·882-0·938) for TLS0, 0·925 (0·899-0·951) for TLS1, and 0·953 (0·933-0·974) for TLS2. For predicting peritoneal recurrence-free survival, the model achieved a concordance index of 0·654 (95% CI 0·620-0·688) in the training cohort. Across all cohorts, patients with low model scores had substantially higher 5-year peritoneal recurrence rates than those with high scores (eg, 66·69%, 95% CI 60·11-73·27 vs 26·28%, 20·05-32·51; p<0·0001 in the training cohort). Multivariate analysis confirmed risk stratification based on the multitask hybrid model score as an independent predictor of peritoneal recurrence-free survival, disease-free survival, and overall survival. Analysis of patients with stage II or stage III disease in the training cohort and internal and external validation cohorts showed that in those with low predicted scores versus high predicted scores, adjuvant chemotherapy was associated with improved disease-free survival and overall survival in patients with low scores but not those with high scores. In the immunotherapy cohorts, objective response rates were higher for patients with high predicted scores than for those with low predicted scores (54·5% vs 5·6%; p<0·0001 in immunotherapy cohort 1 and 53·1% vs 9·7%; p=0·0010 in immunotherapy cohort 2). By accurately predicting tertiary lymphoid structure status, peritoneal recurrence, and survival, the multitask hybrid model shows strong potential as a non-invasive tool for personalised gastric cancer care. The model's potential to identify patients who might benefit from adjuvant chemotherapy and are more likely to respond to immunotherapy could help clinicians to optimise treatment strategies. None.

title: Point-of-care ultrasound in older adults: a scoping review.
abstract: Multimorbidity, non-specific symptoms, and atypical disease manifestations are common in adults aged 65 years or older, complicating diagnostic and prognostic assessment. Point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) provides real-time bedside imaging that can support clinical decision making in this population; however, evidence on its use in older adults has not been systematically mapped. This scoping Review, endorsed by the European Geriatric Medicine Society, mapped POCUS utilisation across health-care settings, application domains, clinical indications, and outcomes. MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science were systematically searched. Eligible studies were peer-reviewed original research articles investigating the use of POCUS in older adults (defined as studies that exclusively enrolled older adults ≥65 years or reported a mixed-age study population with a mean age of 65 years or older) and published in English or another language represented within the review team (Italian, French, German, Spanish, Danish, or Turkish) with no restrictions on publication date. Of the 3897 records, 240 (6%) studies were included; 87 (36%) focused on older adult or geriatric-targeted populations and 153 (64%) on mixed-age populations with a mean age of 65 years or older. Evidence came predominantly from acute care, with few studies in geriatric settings. Thoracic POCUS was the most frequently investigated single-organ domain; multiorgan POCUS was also prominent. Diagnostic support and prognostic stratification predominated, whereas longitudinal monitoring and patient-centred outcomes were infrequent. Evidence on POCUS applications in older adults remains uneven, highlighting the need for further research in under-represented geriatric care settings and on patient-centred outcomes.

title: Radiologic phenotype and the size dependence of adverse histologic features and recurrence in resected lung adenocarcinoma.
abstract: Objectives The eighth edition TNM classification measures part-solid lung adenocarcinoma by the solid component alone. We examined whether CT-measured size carries the same pathologic and prognostic meaning in part-solid and solid adenocarcinoma. Materials and methods We retrospectively analyzed 3857 consecutive patients with resected non-mucinous lung adenocarcinoma (2011-2022), using phenotype and size from preoperative CT reports. Shape-constrained additive models estimated the size-dependent prevalence of seven adverse features, including high-grade (HG) patterns, micropapillary component and spread through air spaces (STAS). Five-year cumulative incidence of recurrence (CIR) was estimated with death as a competing risk. Results Tumors were part-solid in 2100 and solid in 1757 patients. In part-solid tumors, HG patterns, micropapillary component and STAS rose most steeply at 1.25-1.36 cm of total size (0.85-0.93 cm of solid component); in solid tumors, HG patterns and STAS were already frequent at the smallest measured sizes. Lymphovascular, pleural and nodal involvement became prevalent at larger sizes in both phenotypes. Among 3580 patients analyzed for recurrence (467 recurrences; median follow-up, 56.6 months), solid tumors had higher CIR than part-solid tumors within each matched solid-component size stratum (feature-present tumors > 2.5 cm: 42.7% vs 19.6%). In part-solid tumors, 5-year CIR was 1.4% when HG morphology was the most advanced feature, 11.0% with local invasion and 50.0% with nodal involvement. Conclusions Measuring the solid component narrows but does not close the difference in pathologic risk between part-solid and solid adenocarcinoma of the same size. These associations warrant external validation and evaluation in preoperative risk models.
originalAbstract:
Objectives

The eighth edition TNM classification measures part-solid lung adenocarcinoma by the solid component alone. We examined whether CT-measured size carries the same pathologic and prognostic meaning in part-solid and solid adenocarcinoma.

Materials and methods

We retrospectively analyzed 3857 consecutive patients with resected non-mucinous lung adenocarcinoma (2011-2022), using phenotype and size from preoperative CT reports. Shape-constrained additive models estimated the size-dependent prevalence of seven adverse features, including high-grade (HG) patterns, micropapillary component and spread through air spaces (STAS). Five-year cumulative incidence of recurrence (CIR) was estimated with death as a competing risk.

Results

Tumors were part-solid in 2100 and solid in 1757 patients. In part-solid tumors, HG patterns, micropapillary component and STAS rose most steeply at 1.25-1.36 cm of total size (0.85-0.93 cm of solid component); in solid tumors, HG patterns and STAS were already frequent at the smallest measured sizes. Lymphovascular, pleural and nodal involvement became prevalent at larger sizes in both phenotypes. Among 3580 patients analyzed for recurrence (467 recurrences; median follow-up, 56.6 months), solid tumors had higher CIR than part-solid tumors within each matched solid-component size stratum (feature-present tumors > 2.5 cm: 42.7% vs 19.6%). In part-solid tumors, 5-year CIR was 1.4% when HG morphology was the most advanced feature, 11.0% with local invasion and 50.0% with nodal involvement.

Conclusions

Measuring the solid component narrows but does not close the difference in pathologic risk between part-solid and solid adenocarcinoma of the same size. These associations warrant external validation and evaluation in preoperative risk models.

title: ContextMRI: Enhancing compressed sensing MRI through metadata conditioning.
abstract: Compressed sensing MRI seeks to accelerate MRI acquisition processes by sampling fewer k-space measurements and then reconstructing the missing data algorithmically. The success of these approaches often relies on strong priors or learned statistical models. While recent diffusion model-based priors have shown great potential, previous methods typically ignore clinically available metadata (e.g. patient demographics, imaging parameters, slice-specific information). In practice, metadata contains meaningful cues about the anatomy and acquisition protocol, suggesting it could further constrain the reconstruction problem. In this work, we propose ContextMRI, a text-conditioned diffusion model for MRI that integrates granular metadata into the reconstruction process. We train a pixel-space diffusion model directly on minimally processed, complex-valued MRI images. During inference, metadata is converted into a structured text prompt and fed to the model via CLIP text embeddings. By conditioning the prior on metadata, we unlock more accurate reconstructions and show consistent gains across multiple datasets, acceleration factors, and undersampling patterns. Our experiments demonstrate that increasing the fidelity of metadata - ranging from slice location and contrast to patient age, sex, and pathology - systematically boosts reconstruction performance. This work highlights the untapped potential of leveraging clinical context for inverse problems and opens a new direction for metadata-driven MRI reconstruction. Code is available at https://github.com/DoHunLee1/ContextMRI.

title: ISLES'24: Final stroke infarct prediction with multimodal imaging and clinical data. Where do we stand?
abstract: Accurate estimation of brain infarction (i.e., irreversibly damaged tissue) is critical for guiding treatment decisions in acute ischemic stroke. Reliable infarct prediction informs key clinical interventions, including the need for patient transfer to comprehensive stroke centers, the potential benefit of additional reperfusion attempts during mechanical thrombectomy, decisions regarding secondary neuroprotective treatments, and, ultimately, prognosis of clinical outcomes. This work introduces the Ischemic Stroke Lesion Segmentation (ISLES) 2024 challenge, which focuses on the prediction of final infarct volumes from pre-interventional acute stroke imaging and clinical data. ISLES'24 provides a comprehensive, multimodal setting where participants can leverage all clinically and practically available data - including full acute CT imaging, sub-acute follow-up MRI, and structured clinical information - across a train set of N=150 cases. On the hidden test set (N=98), the top-performing model, a multimodal nnU-Net-based architecture, achieved a Dice score of 0.285 ± 0.213 and an absolute volume difference of 21.2 ± 37.2 mL, underlining the significant challenges posed by this task and the need for further advances in multimodal learning. This overview of the ISLES'24 challenge offers two primary contributions: first, it provides a standardized, clinically realistic benchmark for post-treatment infarct prediction, built on a comprehensive, open, and multimodal longitudinal stroke imaging dataset; second, it provides insights into the strengths and limitations of current algorithms and delineates key research directions to guide the development of next-generation infarct prediction models.

title: Pre-training everywhere: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning for medical image analysis via target parameter pre-training.
abstract: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) provides an effective approach for adapting pre-trained models to medical imaging tasks while reducing the number of trainable parameters. Additive PEFT methods freeze the pre-trained backbone and introduce a small set of trainable parameters for downstream adaptation. Although few in number, these parameters form the trainable feature-adaptation pathway and are commonly introduced only when supervised fine-tuning begins. We therefore investigate whether they can benefit from task-relevant preparation before supervised adaptation. To this end, we propose Target Parameter Pre-training (TPP), which introduces an intermediate self-supervised stage for additive PEFT. During this stage, the backbone remains frozen while the target parameters are optimized on the downstream training images through a pretext task. The learned parameters are then used to initialize supervised PEFT. TPP can be integrated with different backbones, pretext tasks, and additive PEFT methods without modifying their inference-time architectures. We evaluate TPP on ten public datasets spanning five imaging modalities and both classification and segmentation tasks. TPP improves most evaluated PEFT-method and dataset combinations, while its effectiveness depends on data alignment, target-data availability, and compatibility between the pretext objective and PEFT architecture. Code will be released at: https://github.com/xl-lei/TPP.

title: LifespanFix: Semi-supervised cortical correction across the human lifespan.
abstract: Accurate characterization of the cerebral cortex in brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is essential for reliable morphometric analyses across the human lifespan. However, the cortex's thin and highly convoluted architecture, together with imaging artifacts, frequently introduces topological and anatomical defects in segmentation that can bias downstream analyses. Here we present LifespanFix, a lifespan-robust cortical correction model that directly fixes topological and anatomical defects in segmentation. Specifically, we develop a semi-supervised framework in which a generation network produces template-constrained pseudo-labels that serve as structurally plausible targets for training a correction network (LifespanFix). During inference, only the trained LifespanFix model is deployed, enabling efficient end-to-end correction of cortical defects without requiring the generation network or the time-intensive registration used during training. Our framework was trained on 3,189 subjects spanning the human lifespan - from infancy to older adulthood - across nine public datasets. For evaluation, we assembled an independent lifespan testing cohort comprising 1,058 subjects from five datasets, including label maps generated by different segmentation methods. LifespanFix consistently outperforms state-of-the-art correction approaches, producing more accurate and anatomically plausible cortical segmentations across diverse ages, scanners, and imaging protocols, thereby enabling more reliable large-scale lifespan neuroimaging analyses.

title: The COSAS 2024 challenge: Cross-Organ and Cross-Scanner Adenocarcinoma Segmentation for domain generalization in computational pathology.
abstract: Histopathological assessment remains the gold standard for cancer diagnosis. However, automated histopathology models can be sensitive to domain shifts arising from organ-specific morphological heterogeneity and scanner-associated acquisition variability. To investigate these complementary sources of variation, we established the Cross-Organ and Cross-Scanner Adenocarcinoma Segmentation (COSAS) 2024 Challenge, comprising separate cross-organ and cross-scanner segmentation tasks. The benchmark includes 580 pixel-level annotated histopathology patches spanning six organ sites and six scanner platforms. Thirty international teams submitted valid solutions using a range of convolutional, transformer-based, and hybrid architectures together with different training, augmentation, and inference strategies. Separately, we evaluated conventional segmentation networks and foundation-model-based baselines as organizer-run references. Performance varied substantially across domains and between the two tasks. The relative strengths of the reference models were task dependent, with no model family uniformly strongest across both settings, while the leading challenge submissions achieved competitive performance through different combinations of augmentation, multi-domain training, model design, and inference-time refinement. Overall, COSAS provides a controlled benchmark for studying cross-domain adenocarcinoma segmentation and offers practical insights into the design of AI systems that can better handle the biological and technical variability encountered in diagnostic workflows.

title: Unsupervised denoising of diffusion-weighted images with bias and variance corrected noise modeling.
abstract: Diffusion magnetic resonance imaging (dMRI) plays a vital role in both clinical diagnostics and neuroscience research. However, its inherently low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), especially under high diffusion weighting, substantially degrades image quality and impairs downstream analysis. Recent self-supervised and unsupervised denoising approaches have shown promising potential without requiring clean reference images. However, most of these methods neglect the non-Gaussian statistical characteristics of noise in magnitude dMRI data, leading to biased estimation and suboptimal optimization under heteroscedastic noise. To address this limitation, we propose two Rician noise-aware loss functions that explicitly account for these characteristics. One loss function is derived from the first-order moment of the Rician distribution for signal bias correction, while the other leverages the second-order moment to perform bias correction through squared-signal statistics. Each loss further incorporates adaptive weighting based on the signal-dependent Rician noise variance to address heteroscedasticity. The proposed objectives are instantiated within an image-specific, unsupervised Deep Image Prior (DIP) framework without modifying the network architecture. Comparisons with state-of-the-art denoising methods on simulated and in vivo dMRI data demonstrate that the proposed approach yields higher image quality and more reliable diffusion metrics. These results highlight the importance of explicitly accounting for Rician noise-induced bias and heteroscedasticity in magnitude-domain dMRI denoising. Code is available at https://github.com/XieJine/Rician-Moment-DIP.

title: Joint-embedding self-supervised representation learning for robust cone-beam CT segmentation.
abstract: Cone-beam CT (CBCT) segmentation is challenged by reconstruction artifacts and limited reliable annotations. We investigate joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA)-style self-supervised learning for volumetric CBCT segmentation using CBCT-LGR, which extends our preliminary slice-wise conference study through fully three-dimensional local-global encoding, learnable semantic tokens, and a combined objective comprising local-global alignment, semantic alignment, and predictive consistency. We compare CBCT-LGR with supervised baselines (nnU-Net and STU-Net), generic self-supervised methods (BYOL-Med3D and Models Genesis), and foundation models (SAM, MedSAM, and Anatomix) using harmonized patient-level splits, preprocessing, and evaluation metrics while retaining each method's stated supervision setting. For representation-learning methods, frozen encoders are evaluated using supervised decoders trained with the same 10-subject labeled-data budget per dataset. Across three datasets, CBCT-LGR outperforms the generic self-supervised baselines on dataset-average overlap and boundary metrics. On CBCTLiTS, supervised and fine-tuned foundation-model approaches achieve higher absolute DSC under clean reconstruction conditions. Across five controlled reconstruction-quality levels, however, CBCT-LGR exhibits the smallest maximum relative DSC decline among all nine methods, with declines of 1.5% for liver and 14.5% for tumor, and achieves the highest numerical tumor DSC at the two most degraded levels. Results on Dataset 1 quantify agreement with imperfect reference annotations and do not establish true anatomical accuracy or a definitive method ranking. These findings define the capabilities and limitations of JEPA-style pretraining for volumetric CBCT segmentation.

title: Confocal microscopy segmentation via prototype-driven semi-supervised learning.
abstract: The segmentation of anatomical structures like corneal nerves and Langerhans cells in in vivo corneal confocal microscopy is vital for diagnosing many ocular and systemic diseases. While deep learning offers a promising path to automation, its clinical translation is hampered by domain shift and a scarcity of labeled data across multi-center cohorts. To address these limitations, we propose Semi-NC, a semi-supervised framework that learns domain-invariant representations from both labeled and unlabeled data through a synergistic, four-step cycle: (1) extracting multi-scale prototype features, (2) refining them via feature amplification regularization, (3) constructing and updating category-specific prototype pools by aggregating features, and (4) aligning pixels to prototypes via contrastive learning to optimize the feature space for precise segmentation. Extensive evaluations on seven datasets (10,987 images across 22 diseases) show that Semi-NC sets a new state-of-the-art, outperforming fully-supervised baselines with minimal labels. The framework also demonstrates strong generalization under in-distribution and out-of-distribution tests, along with a robust self-evolution capability that allows it to extend its functionality using unseen data while preserving performance on learned tasks. Its broad clinical utility is further validated by superior performance on retinal optical coherence tomography angiography. To support reproducibility, we will open-source the code and the first multi-center, multi-disease dataset with high-quality annotations at https://github.com/iMED-Lab/Semi-NC.

title: Imaging-detected extranodal extension grading and T-category adjustment to refine the TNM-9 classification for nasopharyngeal carcinoma.
abstract: Background The ninth edition of the TNM classification (TNM-9) for nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) has been implemented but requires further validation and refinement. Methods A multicenter retrospective cohort of 6,049 patients with nonmetastatic NPC treated with intensity-modulated radiotherapy (IMRT) (2016-2017) was analyzed. Patients were restaged from TNM-8 to TNM-9 using pretreatment MRI. Overall survival (OS) was the primary endpoint. Prognostic performance was compared using multivariable Cox regression and Groome's criteria. Early skull base invasion (ESBI), cranial nerve foramen invasion (CNFI), and grade 2 imaging-detected extranodal extension (G2-iENE) were evaluated as potential refinements. Findings TNM-9 outperformed TNM-8 according to Groome's criteria, but category distribution remained imbalanced (T3, 44.3%; N1, 48.0%), and survival separation between T2 and T3 was limited despite statistical significance (5-year OS, 90.0% vs. 88.0%; p = 0.006). For the TNM-9 T category, T3_ESBI showed OS similar to T2 (adjusted hazard ratio [aHR] = 1.01, 95% confidence interval [CI] = 0.76-1.34, p = 0.94), whereas T3_CNFI demonstrated OS similar to T4 disease (aHR = 1.11, 95% CI = 0.85-1.44, p = 0.44). For the N category, N1_G2-iENE and N2 disease also had similar OS (aHR = 1.03, 95% CI = 0.79-1.34, p = 0.82). Reclassifying T3_ESBI as T2, T3_CNFI as T4, and N1_G2-iENE as N2 improved hazard discrimination and sample balance versus TNM-9. Conclusions Although TNM-9 outperforms TNM-8, limitations remain in T- and N-category discrimination and distribution balance. Incorporating ESBI, CNFI, and G2-iENE into the staging framework improves prognostic performance for NPC. Background

The ninth edition of the TNM classification (TNM-9) for nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) has been implemented but requires further validation and refinement.

Methods

A multicenter retrospective cohort of 6,049 patients with nonmetastatic NPC treated with intensity-modulated radiotherapy (IMRT) (2016-2017) was analyzed. Patients were restaged from TNM-8 to TNM-9 using pretreatment MRI. Overall survival (OS) was the primary endpoint. Prognostic performance was compared using multivariable Cox regression and Groome's criteria. Early skull base invasion (ESBI), cranial nerve foramen invasion (CNFI), and grade 2 imaging-detected extranodal extension (G2-iENE) were evaluated as potential refinements.

Findings

TNM-9 outperformed TNM-8 according to Groome's criteria, but category distribution remained imbalanced (T3, 44.3%; N1, 48.0%), and survival separation between T2 and T3 was limited despite statistical significance (5-year OS, 90.0% vs. 88.0%; p = 0.006). For the TNM-9 T category, T3_ESBI showed OS similar to T2 (adjusted hazard ratio [aHR] = 1.01, 95% confidence interval [CI] = 0.76-1.34, p = 0.94), whereas T3_CNFI demonstrated OS similar to T4 disease (aHR = 1.11, 95% CI = 0.85-1.44, p = 0.44). For the N category, N1_G2-iENE and N2 disease also had similar OS (aHR = 1.03, 95% CI = 0.79-1.34, p = 0.82). Reclassifying T3_ESBI as T2, T3_CNFI as T4, and N1_G2-iENE as N2 improved hazard discrimination and sample balance versus TNM-9.

Conclusions

Although TNM-9 outperforms TNM-8, limitations remain in T- and N-category discrimination and distribution balance. Incorporating ESBI, CNFI, and G2-iENE into the staging framework improves prognostic performance for NPC.

title: Three-dimensional analysis of human craniofacial development between 6 and 15weeks of gestation using diffusible iodine-based contrast-enhanced micro-computed tomography.
abstract: Human craniofacial development has traditionally been studied by histology, which is detailed but destructive and limits multiplanar examination. Quantitative three-dimensional (3D) morphometric and volumetric approaches can characterise the spatial relationships and growth of craniofacial structures during early human development. In this study, diffusible iodine-based contrast-enhanced (DICE) micro-computed tomography (micro-CT) was used as an established imaging platform to quantify these developmental changes. To quantitatively characterise human craniofacial development using DICE micro-CT, and to assess its concordance with established histological and micro-CT-based descriptions of palatogenesis. Twenty-three human embryonic and fetal specimens (6.7-14.4weeks of gestation [WG]) from termination of pregnancy underwent DICE micro-CT; standardised anatomical landmarks were defined for linear and angular measurements. Tongue, palate and mandible were manually segmented in 12 specimens for 3D and volumetric analysis. DICE micro-CT allowed high-resolution multiplanar and 3D visualisation within the same specimen. Findings were consistent with established histological descriptions. Early specimens showed a high tongue and vertical palatal processes; around 10-11WG, tongue horizontalization, mandibular growth and palatal process elevation occurred, followed by palatal closure. Cranial base flexion and predominantly anterior cranial growth were also demonstrated. Volumes increased with gestational age, with an apparent, descriptive change in growth rate around 9-11 WG. Quantitative morphometric and volumetric analysis complements histological descriptions of early human craniofacial development and provides preliminary data for future 3D reference studies. Micro-CT reproduces established histological observations, providing a basis for morphological references and future applications in research, teaching and fetal post-mortem examination.

title: Orbital morphometry on computed tomography for sex estimation: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
abstract: Computed tomography (CT)-based orbital morphometry has been investigated for sex estimation, although diagnostic performance varies across populations and measurement protocols. The aim was to systematically review CT-based studies that assess orbital morphometry for sex estimation in adults and, when feasible, synthesize diagnostic performance measures. The review protocol was registered on the Open Science Framework, and the review was reported according to PRISMA guidelines. Comprehensive searches were performed, and eligible studies evaluated orbital sexual dimorphism in adults using CT imaging. Study selection and data extraction were performed independently by two reviewers. Risk of bias was assessed using the AQUA tool. Sensitivity and specificity were synthesized using bivariate models where estimable; otherwise simplified models were used. Accuracy was synthesized using logit-scale random-effects models. Eleven studies were included, and eight contributed data to the quantitative syntheses. The main syntheses included five biorbital width studies and six of orbital height. Among the retained linear-measure datasets, individual-study accuracy ranged from 50.00% to 83.77%, sensitivity from 53.77% to 84.00%, and specificity from 44.00% to 86.40%. For biorbital width, pooled sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy were 71.65%, 65.95%, and 68.14%, respectively. Corresponding estimates for orbital height were 62.98%, 65.78%, and 64.02%. Accuracy confidence intervals were 56.39-77.97% and 48.96-76.74%, respectively, with substantial heterogeneity in both syntheses. Several studies reported higher classification accuracy with multivariable models, while methodological characterization represented the main source of bias. Certainty of evidence ranged from very low to low. Overall, CT-based orbital morphometry shows sexual dimorphism. However, it should be used as a complementary tool for sex estimation.

title: Retraining-free multi-task MR image restoration using a pretrained diffusion model with Bayesian optimization.
abstract: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) often requires long scan times, and efforts to shorten scans can lead to image degradation, such as undersampling artifacts, increased noise, and reduced spatial resolution. A restoration framework that can address multiple types of degradation without task-specific retraining would therefore be valuable. In this study, we evaluated whether a pretrained score-based diffusion model combined with Bayesian optimization, termed task guidance design with Bayesian optimization (TGD-BO), could provide retraining-free, multi-task MR image restoration for compressed sensing (CS) reconstruction, super-resolution (SR), and denoising (DN). TGD-BO incorporates data-consistency guidance and gradient guidance into the reverse diffusion process and parameterizes their time-varying strengths using compact low-dimensional B-spline-based guidance schedules. For each task, the schedule was optimized by Bayesian optimization using four paired degraded/reference slices from a single adaptation case, and the resulting task-specific schedule was then applied unchanged to an independent test set. In single-task experiments, TGD-BO improved upon the fixed-guidance diffusion baseline in denoising, compressed-sensing reconstruction, and super-resolution, although the improvement in super-resolution was modest. Compared with task-specific supervised baselines, TGD-BO did not uniformly achieve higher peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) or structural similarity (SSIM); in super-resolution, it showed lower PSNR and SSIM but better perceptual similarity as assessed by learned perceptual image patch similarity (LPIPS). In joint-task experiments, schedules optimized directly for DN + CS and DN + SR yielded numerically better image-quality metrics than applying the corresponding single-task schedules. Sensitivity analyses showed that the selected schedule and test performance were unchanged when 1, 4, or 8 slices from the same adaptation case were used, whereas changing the adaptation case substantially affected test performance. These results suggest the feasibility of adapting a single pretrained diffusion prior across multiple MR image restoration tasks through guidance calibration without task-specific weight retraining, while indicating that robustness to adaptation-case selection and computational cost require further investigation.

title: Measurement-derived residual-risk verification through four-way k-space partitioning in self-supervised accelerated brain MRI.
abstract: Self-supervised accelerated MRI reconstruction reduces dependence on fully sampled training targets, but it does not inherently provide a separate basis for verifying whether reconstructed image content remains locally consistent with acquired measurements. We developed a measurement-derived verification framework that partitions acquired k-space into four roles: reconstruction input, self-supervised reconstruction-loss evaluation, residual-risk learning, and reserved verification. Residuals from the reserved measurements were transformed into spatial residual-risk targets using density-compensated adjoint projection, probe-based gain normalization, anatomical support weighting, percentile scaling, and logarithmic compression. Using fastMRI brain multicoil data, we evaluated 201 training, 40 calibration, and 40 AXT2 test volumes, comprising 636 test slices and 999,792 sampled pixels. The primary Full-CNN achieved AUPRC 0.8348, mean absolute error 0.0834, Spearman correlation 0.9389, and AUROC 0.9818. The secondary A4-CNN achieved AUPRC 0.8452 with similar scale and rank agreement. MRI-volume intervals achieved at least 90% sampled-location coverage in 39 of 40 test volumes for both predictors. AUPRC declined and MAE increased with fewer reserved measurements and under AXFLAIR sequence shift. Residual-risk maps showed moderate correspondence with fully sampled reference error and differed from the tested predictive-variance measures. The framework provides a measurement-derived verification layer for assessing local residual inconsistency in self-supervised accelerated MRI without requiring fully sampled development targets.

title: Diffusion tensor imaging and structural MRI reveal early microstructural injury and progressive atrophy of the olfactory bulb in type 1 diabetic rats.
abstract: Purpose To determine whether diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) can detect early olfactory bulb microstructural abnormalities in streptozotocin (STZ)-induced type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM) rats and to investigate their relationship with structural and histopathological changes. Methods Control and STZ-induced T1DM rats underwent DTI, high-resolution structural MRI and histological examination at 2 and 12 weeks after model induction. Fractional anisotropy (FA), mean diffusivity (MD), axial diffusivity (Da), and radial diffusivity (Dr) were measured in the olfactory nerve layer/glomerular layer/external plexiform layer (ONL/GL/EPL), granule cell layer (GCL), and subependymal zone (SEZ). Results Compared to the controls, T1DM rats showed decreased FA and increased MD, Da, and Dr in the ONL/GL/EPL at 2 and 12 weeks after model induction. In the GCL, FA was decreased, whereas Dr was increased. No significant diffusion abnormalities were detected in the SEZ. Ultrastructural examination revealed axolemmal disruption, demyelination, reduced axoplasmic content, and axonal vacuolization in the ONL. Voxel-based morphometry (VBM) demonstrated olfactory bulb atrophy as early as 2 weeks, initially involving the GCL and SEZ, with more extensive and regionally heterogeneous atrophy at 12 weeks. Nissl staining confirmed structural atrophy, and increased caspase-3 immunoreactivity supported apoptosis-related tissue injury. STZ-induced T1DM causes early, layer-specific olfactory bulb microstructural abnormalities and progressive structural atrophy. Conclusion The differing spatial and temporal distributions of diffusion abnormalities and atrophy suggest that DTI and volumetric MRI capture partially distinct aspects of diabetes-associated olfactory bulb injury. DTI may provide a sensitive, noninvasive approach for detecting early microstructural abnormalities before widespread structural loss develops.

title: HSMD: A Hilbert-scanning mamba dense network for 3D MRI reconstruction.
abstract: Long MRI acquisition times motivate the use of k-space undersampling for accelerated imaging, but undersampling often introduces aliasing artifacts and structural detail loss. Existing 2D slice-wise reconstruction methods fail to fully exploit inter-slice anatomical correlations. This study develops a Hilbert-Scanning Mamba Dense Network (HSMD) for high-quality 3D MRI reconstruction, which leverages inter-slice contextual information to improve reconstruction fidelity. The proposed HSMD consists of a Shallow Feature Extraction Module (SFEM) and five cascaded Multi-Directional Spatial Attention (MDSA) modules. The SFEM is responsible for extracting local detailed features and coarse-scale structural context from undersampled MRI inputs. The MDSA modules extract and fuse multi-directional spatial information along the depth, height, and width dimensions to enhance the representation of 3D structural features. Furthermore, a multi-directional Hilbert selective state-space scanning strategy is introduced into MDSA to capture long-range spatial dependencies within 3D volumetric data, thereby improving structural representation while preserving spatial locality. Experimental results on the BraTS and UCSF-PDGM datasets under diverse acceleration factors validate that the proposed HSMD achieves superior performance over state-of-the-art methods in both quantitative metrics and visual quality. The HSMD exhibits excellent capability in 3D undersampled MRI reconstruction, holding promising prospects for efficient and reliable clinical MRI applications.

title: Deep learning-derived functional MRI connectivity maps of cervical spinal cord segments during hand grasping.
abstract: Task-based fMRI of the cervical spinal cord is limited by physiological noise and small sample sizes. The primary objective of this study was to examine whether a convolutional neural network (CNN)-based denoising framework can improve the detection of task-dependent functional connectivity between cervical spinal segments using generalized psychophysiological interaction (gPPI) analysis. An open dataset of 26 healthy adults performing a hand-grasp task with alternating right- and left-hand blocks during 3 T fMRI was analyzed. A CNN with Inception V3 transfer learning (91.0% slice-level and 89.2% block-level accuracy) was trained to classify grasp versus rest, and the trained model was then utilized to derive denoised time series from masks of the spinal segments C5-C8. A gPPI model with a C6 ventral horn seed was evaluated using FDR correction and permutation testing (n = 1000). C6 showed positive task-dependent connectivity with C7 (β = 0.72, p = 0.003) and C8 (β = 0.58, p = 0.018), and negative connectivity with C5 (β = -0.31, p = 0.041), which is broadly consistent with the organization of the cervical myotomes. The C6-C5 effect was marginal and was not detected when conventional time series were used (p = 0.21), and therefore it requires replication. Grad-CAM maps aligned with ventral horn motor pools (Dice = 0.89 at C7). These results suggest that deep learning-based denoising may increase the sensitivity of spinal cord fMRI to segmental connectivity, although validation in larger cohorts is needed.

title: Integrated deep learning reconstruction combining phase correction, denoising, and super-resolution for prostate diffusion-weighted imaging.
abstract: Objective To evaluate integrated deep learning reconstruction (Integrated DLR), which combines phase correction, denoising, and super-resolution, for prostate diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) by comparing it with compressed sensing (CS) and deep learning-based denoising reconstruction (Denoising DLR). Methods This single-center, retrospective study included 47 patients scanned on a single-vendor 3-T system. Three DWI datasets were reconstructed from identical raw data using CS, Denoising DLR, and Integrated DLR. Two radiologists rated overall image quality, noise, artifact, and prostate delineation. Apparent signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) was assessed in all patients. In 21 patients with pathologically confirmed prostate cancer, we assessed lesion conspicuity, lesion localization/anatomical relationship, Prostate Imaging Reporting and Data System (PI-RADS) version 2.1 DWI scores, apparent lesion contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR), and apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC). Comparisons were performed using Friedman tests followed by Bonferroni-corrected Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. Results Scores for overall image quality, noise, and prostate delineation were highest with Integrated DLR, followed by Denoising DLR and CS, for both readers (all p < 0.001); apparent SNR showed the same pattern (p < 0.001). Artifact scores did not differ among methods. Lesion conspicuity differed among methods for Reader 2 (p = 0.044) but not for Reader 1 (p = 0.199), whereas Integrated DLR yielded the highest lesion localization/anatomical relationship scores for both readers (both p < 0.001). Integrated DLR also yielded the highest apparent CNR and lesion ADC (both p < 0.001), while PI-RADS DWI scores were unchanged. Conclusion Integrated DLR improved prostate DWI image quality and lesion visibility compared with CS and Denoising DLR, potentially facilitating visual assessment of prostate DWI.

title: Tensor-based dynamic MRI reconstruction with non-convex ℓ<sub>r</sub><sup>p</sup> pseudo-norm and adaptive weighting.
abstract: Compressed sensing significantly accelerates dynamic magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) by undersampling (k, t)-space, thereby formulating an ill-posed inverse problem that heavily depends on reconstruction algorithms. Dynamic MRI data exhibit low-rank property due to strong correlations in both spatial and temporal dimensions. In this paper, we propose a tensor-based ℓ r p pseudo-norm regularization for low-rank dynamic MRI reconstruction model, and introduce the weighting mechanism to adaptively distinguish between signal and noise, termed as TNWLR. We take tensor as processing unit to protect the inherent structure and facilitate the exploitation of its inherent structural correlations. The utilization of tensor-based ℓ r p pseudo-norm adequately exploits the spatial and temporal redundancies, and provides a flexible non-convex approximation to the rank function. In addition, using the weighting mechanism enables the suppression of noise and artifacts while better preserving the low-rank structure. The alternating direction multiplier method (ADMM) provides an efficient solution framework for the proposed model due to its ability to decouple complex constraints. Compared with representative reconstruction methods, extensive experiments on multi-coil brain and liver DCE-MRI datasets demonstrate improved quantitative performance and better visual preservation of anatomical structures and fine details, and strong robustness to noise.

title: Ultra-High-Field (7T) knee MRI: review of technical considerations and current evidence, with experience from an institutional clinical series.
abstract: Background Ultra-high-field, 7 Tesla (T) MRI provides higher signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and enables high-resolution 3D and quantitative imaging. Its role in musculoskeletal (MSK) knee imaging is emerging but not yet standardized. Purpose To review current 7 T knee MRI techniques and evidence, detail key technical/physics considerations, and to report a single-center clinical experience through a descriptive study. Methods Up to date narrative synthesis of the literature organized by qualitative (morphologic) and quantitative applications, complemented by experience from a retrospective single-center series of consecutive 7 T knee examinations. Results Literature shows that 7 T imaging can improve conspicuity of cartilage, meniscus, ligaments, and bone microarchitecture with isotropic 3D acquisitions; quantitative methods (T2/T2*, Ultrashort Echo Time (UTE), Glycosaminoglycan Chemical Exchange Saturation Transfer (gagCEST), 23 Na, T1rho) show promise but require rigorous B0/B1 correction and Specific Absorption Rate (SAR) management. Our experience demonstrated that 7 T imaging was clinically feasible and well tolerated in a cohort of 131 patients (mean age 33.8 ± 10.5 years ranging from 16 to 63 years) and provided a potential and a subjective increase in diagnosis confidence in selected scenarios, particularly in postoperative meniscus assessment and conservative ACL follow-up. Conclusion 7 T knee MRI is feasible and potentially impactful in specific indications; however, stronger comparative data, protocol harmonization, and quantitative validation are needed.

title: Ultra-low-field MRI assesses brain volumes and age-related changes: validation against high-field MRI.
abstract: Objective High-field MRI is the standard for assessing brain atrophy in neurodegenerative disorders, but limited access can restrict research and clinical care, particularly outside urban centers. Portable ultra-low-field (ULF) MRI may improve access, but their suitability for quantitative morphometry and detection of neurodegenerative-related atrophy is not well established. We evaluated agreement between 64 mT ULF MRI and 3T MRI for brain volumetric measurements and explored their potential utility in neurodegenerative disorders. Methods We conducted a prospective, cross-sectional study of adults, including patients with neurodegenerative, subacute stroke, and healthy controls. Participants underwent both 3T and 64 mT ULF MRI with T1-weighted imaging. Regional brain volumes were extracted from both modalities using WMH-SynthSeg. Agreement between ULF- and 3T-derived volumes were assessed using intraclass correlation coefficients and Bland-Altman analyses. Where applicable, 3T FreeSurfer-derived volumes were used as an additional reference standard. Analyses in the neurodegenerative disorder subgroup were considered exploratory because the subgroup was not powered for formal inferential comparisons. Results ULF and 3T volumetric measures show variable agreement (ICC ranged from 0.29 to 0.95), with the highest agreement for large structures such as total ventricles (ICC 0.85 to 0.95) and the lowest for the Pallidum (ICC 0.34 to 0.51). Age-related trajectories of gray and white matter decline, and ventricular expansion show the same pattern for WMH-SynthSeg and FreeSurfer-derived volumes. Exploratory analysis suggests pathological atrophy might differ from healthy aging trajectories. Interpretation Portable ultra-low-field MRI combined with automated segmentation produced brain volumetric estimates that were broadly consistent with 3T MRI, particularly for larger structures relevant to atrophy assessment. These findings support the feasibility of ultra-low-field MRI for accessible morphometric evaluation in clinical research and potentially in under-resourced settings. Larger, adequately powered studies are needed to define diagnostic accuracy, prediction intervals, and clinical utility in specific neurodegenerative disorder populations.

title: Preoperative prediction of HER2 status in breast cancer using multiparametric MRI deep learning and clinical features.
abstract: Background HER2 status is an important biomarker in breast cancer, but its assessment primarily relies on core needle biopsy and pathological examination. Therefore, noninvasive preoperative prediction of HER2 status has important clinical value. This study aimed to evaluate the predictive value of models integrating multiparametric MRI deep learning, radiomics, and clinical features for preoperative HER2 status prediction in breast cancer. Materials and methods A total of 257 patients with pathologically confirmed breast cancer were retrospectively enrolled, including 98 HER2-positive and 159 HER2-negative patients. All patients underwent preoperative T1WI, T2WI, DWI, and DCE-MRI. Patients were randomly divided at the patient level into training (n = 174) and internal test (n = 83) cohorts at a 7:3 ratio. Cli, Rad, and DL models were constructed based on clinical, radiomics, and deep learning features, respectively, along with single-sequence fusion models. Subsequently, an mpMRI model integrating radiomics and deep learning features from all four MRI sequences and an mpMRI_Cli model further incorporating statistically significant preoperative clinical features were developed. Model performance was evaluated using the AUC, accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, negative predictive value, F1 score, Brier score, decision curve analysis, calibration curves, and confusion matrices. DeLong's test was used to compare AUCs between models. Results In the internal test cohort, the AUCs of the T1WI, T2WI, DWI, and DCE-MRI models were 0.666, 0.689, 0.710, and 0.728, respectively. The AUCs of the Cli, Rad, and DL models were 0.571, 0.764, and 0.791, respectively. The mpMRI model achieved an AUC of 0.910 (95% CI: 0.837-0.966), with an accuracy of 0.831, sensitivity of 0.742, and specificity of 0.885. The mpMRI_Cli model achieved an AUC of 0.923 (95% CI: 0.860-0.972), with an accuracy of 0.819, sensitivity of 0.839, specificity of 0.808, and Brier score of 0.122. Although the mpMRI_Cli model had a higher AUC than the mpMRI model, the difference was not statistically significant after Holm correction (P = 0.744). Conclusion Integrating multiparametric MRI radiomics and deep learning features improved preoperative prediction of HER2 status in breast cancer. Further incorporation of clinical features increased the AUC and sensitivity and reduced the Brier score, although the improvement in AUC was not statistically significant. Both models show potential for noninvasive preoperative HER2 prediction, but further validation in independent external and multicenter cohorts is warranted.

title: Active negative loss: A robust framework for learning with noisy labels.
abstract: Deep supervised learning has achieved remarkable success across a wide range of tasks, yet it remains susceptible to overfitting when confronted with noisy labels. To address this issue, noise-robust loss functions offer an effective solution for enhancing learning in the presence of label noise. In this work, we systematically investigate the limitation of the recently proposed Active Passive Loss (APL), which employs Mean Absolute Error (MAE) as its passive loss function. Despite the robustness brought by MAE, one of its key drawbacks is that it pays equal attention to clean and noisy samples; this feature slows down convergence and potentially makes training difficult, particularly in large-scale datasets. To overcome these challenges, we introduce a novel loss function class, termed Normalized Negative Loss Functions (NNLFs), which serve as passive loss functions within the APL framework. NNLFs effectively address the limitations of MAE by concentrating more on memorized clean samples. By replacing MAE in APL with our proposed NNLFs, we enhance APL and present a new framework called Active Negative Loss (ANL). Moreover, in non-symmetric noise scenarios, we propose an entropy-based regularization technique to mitigate the vulnerability to the label imbalance. Our experiments demonstrate competitive performance against representative robust-loss methods across the evaluated symmetric, asymmetric, instance-dependent, and real-world label-noise settings. In addition, we evaluate the ANL framework on two medical image segmentation benchmarks, ISIC-2017 and GlaS, under noisy mask annotations. The source code of our method is available at: https://github.com/xichenye0930/Active-Negative-Loss.

title: BH-CDiff: Boundary-aware and heterogeneous feature synergy cold diffusion for medical image segmentation.
abstract: Recently, diffusion models have shown significant potential for medical image segmentation, providing improved interpretability through their iterative optimization process. To address the uncertainty introduced by Gaussian noise in traditional diffusion methods, the cold diffusion paradigm replaces stochastic noise with task-relevant perturbations, enabling more controllable mask generation. However, existing cold diffusion-based segmentation methods still face challenges in recovering boundary structures during iterative restoration and effectively exploiting dynamically evolving heterogeneous representations. This paper proposes a boundary-aware and heterogeneous feature synergy cold diffusion network (BH-CDiff). Specifically, we introduce a boundary-aware modeling mechanism through the boundary-aware feature modulation (BAFM) module, which uses boundary priors to guide channel-spatial attention and effectively enhance boundary information. The heterogeneous feature synergy mechanism is realized through the multi-domain representation synergy (MDRS) module and the dual-source feature fusion (DSFF) module. The former jointly models frequency-domain and spatial-domain features for synergistic multi-domain representation, while the latter fuses segmentation features with conditional priors to promote complementary enhancement of dual-source information. Extensive experiments on the ISIC 2018, CVC-ClinicDB, and REFUGE datasets demonstrate that the proposed method attains state-of-the-art results.

title: NA-DIP: A Noise-Aware Deep Image Prior for Generating Dedicated Brain PET-Quality Images from Whole-Body PET Acquisitions.
abstract: Purpose To generate dedicated brain PET-quality images from routine whole-body PET acquisitions by robustly enhancing the brain region using a noise-aware deep image prior (NA-DIP) approach. Methods NA-DIP integrates anatomy-guided priors derived from patient-specific μ-maps or MR images, a regularization strategy for enhanced denoising, and a variance-based early stopping criterion that adaptively monitors noise without requiring prior noise assumptions. Using noisy PET images as self-supervised targets, the method was first evaluated using simulation data spanning three noise levels to investigate the trade-off between noise suppression and bias. It was then applied to brain images extracted from 90-s-per-bed-position whole-body acquisitions from 15 pediatric FDG-PET studies spanning a broad range of patient demographics, physiological variability, and image noise levels. Using the corresponding 360-s-per-bed-position dedicated brain scans as the reference, NA-DIP-enhanced images were evaluated for noise reduction, standardized uptake value (SUV) accuracy, and image quality in a blinded reader study. Results NA-DIP demonstrated a superior noise-bias trade-off compared with Gaussian filtering and conventional DIP stopping strategies, particularly under high-noise conditions. The inclusion of MR or μ-map guidance further improved performance. Across pediatric patients, NA-DIP-enhanced 90-s images exhibited lower noise than the corresponding 360-s dedicated brain images while showing modest variability in SUV measurements. Blinded readers rated the NA-DIP-enhanced images as comparable to or better than dedicated brain images in most cases. Conclusion NA-DIP enhanced brain PET images from whole-body acquisitions demonstrated good quantitative agreement and image quality comparable to or exceeding the reference, supporting the feasibility of eliminating separate dedicated brain scans.

originalAbstract:
Purpose

To generate dedicated brain PET-quality images from routine whole-body PET acquisitions by robustly enhancing the brain region using a noise-aware deep image prior (NA-DIP) approach.

Methods

NA-DIP integrates anatomy-guided priors derived from patient-specific μ-maps or MR images, a regularization strategy for enhanced denoising, and a variance-based early stopping criterion that adaptively monitors noise without requiring prior noise assumptions. Using noisy PET images as self-supervised targets, the method was first evaluated using simulation data spanning three noise levels to investigate the trade-off between noise suppression and bias. It was then applied to brain images extracted from 90-s-per-bed-position whole-body acquisitions from 15 pediatric FDG-PET studies spanning a broad range of patient demographics, physiological variability, and image noise levels. Using the corresponding 360-s-per-bed-position dedicated brain scans as the reference, NA-DIP-enhanced images were evaluated for noise reduction, standardized uptake value (SUV) accuracy, and image quality in a blinded reader study.

Results

NA-DIP demonstrated a superior noise-bias trade-off compared with Gaussian filtering and conventional DIP stopping strategies, particularly under high-noise conditions. The inclusion of MR or μ-map guidance further improved performance. Across pediatric patients, NA-DIP-enhanced 90-s images exhibited lower noise than the corresponding 360-s dedicated brain images while showing modest variability in SUV measurements. Blinded readers rated the NA-DIP-enhanced images as comparable to or better than dedicated brain images in most cases.

Conclusion

NA-DIP enhanced brain PET images from whole-body acquisitions demonstrated good quantitative agreement and image quality comparable to or exceeding the reference, supporting the feasibility of eliminating separate dedicated brain scans.

title: Accurate 3D brain cross-modality image translation by lesion-aware post-training of latent diffusion models with voxel-space objectives.
abstract: Cross-modality image synthesis offers significant potential for mitigating challenges in medical image acquisition, particularly in acute settings. While latent diffusion models (LDMs) currently represent the state-of-the-art in generative modeling by leveraging compressed latent spaces, this efficiency necessitates a trade-off that often compromises fine structural details. This limitation is particularly critical when reconstructing small but clinically significant structures, such as ischemic lesions, where high-fidelity delineation is essential for diagnostic utility. To address this challenge, we propose a novel post-training framework for LDMs in 3D medical image-to-image translation by incorporating lesion-aware medical voxel-space objectives (LDM-3D-LAPT). Specifically, we convert the pretrained 2D LDM into a 3D volumetric model and post-train the model using a multi-objective loss function incorporating global image reconstruction, focal lesion-specific reconstruction, and auxiliary lesion segmentation guidance. We evaluate this framework on the task of synthesizing diffusion MRI from CT perfusion scans in a cohort of 100 acute ischemic stroke patients. We further evaluate our framework in an independent external cohort of 85 patients. Ablation studies showed that voxel-space post-training improved lesion segmentation. Internal and external evaluations demonstrated gains in ADC lesion fidelity and lesion-detection sensitivity. Our adaptable post-training strategy provides a practical approach to improving lesion-focused medical image translation.

title: An approximation of MRI R 2 * as a rapid surrogate of nigral iron in Parkinson's disease.
abstract: Nigral iron accumulation is a robust imaging marker of Parkinson's disease and is commonly assessed using R 2 * mapping. However, its clinical implementation is limited by long acquisition times. An alternative metric, effective R 2 , derived from dual-contrast proton density- and T2-weighted MRI, has recently been proposed as a fast surrogate of tissue iron content. Using data from the Parkinson's Progression Markers Initiative (PPMI), we evaluated the diagnostic and longitudinal performance of effective R 2 in the substantia nigra (SN) across multiple scanner platforms. Cross-sectional analysis demonstrated significantly higher effective R 2 values in de novo Parkinson's disease patients (n = 187) compared with prodromal subjects (n = 26), with consistent effects across acquisition protocols. In Siemens data (177 patients and 25 prodromal subjects), effective R 2 achieved good discriminative performance for Parkinson's disease classification (AUC = 0.85). Longitudinal analysis for 14 patients over 36 months showed no significant change in effective R 2 values despite clinical progression measured by MDS-UPDRS Part III scores. These findings indicate that effective R 2 provides robust cross-sectional discrimination of early Parkinson's disease but with limited sensitivity to disease progression.

title: Choroid plexus remodeling in aging and cerebrovascular disease revealed by contrast-enhanced 7T MRI.
abstract: Background The choroid plexus is essential for brain homeostasis, yet its in vivo morphology remains incompletely characterized. Conventional MRI visualizes only part of the choroid plexus and may therefore misrepresent age- and disease-related structural changes. We aim to develop a 7T contrast-enhanced black-blood imaging (CeBBI) framework for whole-brain visualization and quantitative morphologic characterization of the choroid plexus, and to examine its associations with aging and cerebrovascular disease. Methods We retrospectively included 234 participants referred for evaluation of intracranial atherosclerotic disease who underwent CeBBI. A deep learning model was trained to segment the whole choroid plexus. Choroid plexus volume, centerline-based shape features and cystic components were quantified. Segmentations derived from CeBBI were compared with those obtained using a validated T1-weighted MRI-based method. Associations with age, ventricular size and vascular imaging markers were assessed. Results 7T CeBBI enabled visualization of the choroid plexus across all ventricular compartments. The segmentation model achieved high accuracy (Dice score=0.901±0.013), and recovered more than twice the choroid plexus volume detected by the T1-weighted method. Total choroid plexus volume was not associated with age. However, with advancing age, the lateral ventricular choroid plexus became shorter (left r=-0.250, right r=-0.303, both P<0.001) and showed greater cross-sectional area (left r=0.174, right r=0.176, both P=0.007). Choroid plexus cyst number (r=0.187, P=0.004) and cyst volume (r=0.159, P=0.015) also increased with age. Cerebral microbleeds were independently associated with greater lateral ventricular choroid plexus volume (standardized β=0.178, P=0.012). Conclusions Our method enables robust whole-brain visualization and quantitative morphologic assessment of the choroid plexus. Rather than undergoing simple age-related hypertrophy, the choroid plexus showed complex remodeling characterized by shortening, cross-sectional expansion and cystic change. The association between cerebral microbleeds and larger choroid plexus volume further supports a potential role of vascular dysfunction in choroid plexus remodeling.

title: Multimodal MRI reveals brain structural and functional abnormalities associated with wearing-off phenomenon in Parkinson's disease.
abstract: Objectives The pathogenesis of the wearing-off (WO) phenomenon in Parkinson's disease (PD) remains unclear. This study aims to explore the abnormalities in brain structure and function among PD patients with WO. Methods A total of 39 PD patients with wearing-off (PD-WO) and 43 PD patients without wearing-off (PD-nWO) were prospectively enrolled. Voxel-based morphometry (VBM) was employed in this study to evaluate structural differences, and functional connectivity (FC) was used to assess functional differences between the two groups. Results Compared with PD-nWO patients, PD-WO patients showed significantly reduced gray matter volume (GMV) within the left middle occipital gyrus (MOG.L), bilateral middle temporal gyri (MTG.L/R), as well as the left triangular division of the inferior frontal gyrus (IFGtriang.L). Regarding functional connectivity, PD-WO patients exhibited widespread abnormalities, including weakened connectivity in the cerebellar-basal ganglia-sensorimotor cortex circuits, hippocampus-postcentral gyrus, and cerebellar-occipital (cuneal cortex) pathways, as well as enhanced connectivity between cerebellar subregions and between the cerebellum and occipital cortex (lingual gyrus) and parahippocampal gyrus. Conclusions This preliminary single-center cross-sectional study revealed significant differences in brain structure and function between PD-WO and PD-nWO patients. These findings provide a better understanding of the neural mechanisms behind the WO phenomenon in PD and suggest potential therapeutic targets.

title: Cerebellar structural and electrophysiological alterations associated with neuropathic pain in mice.
abstract: The cerebellum is increasingly implicated in pain, yet direct electrophysiology in neuropathy is scarce. We tested whether sciatic nerve chronic constriction injury (CCI) alters cerebellar dynamics and structure. Adult male mice underwent CCI, von Frey testing, structural MRI, spontaneous LFP recordings in lobules IV-V, and spontaneous/evoked single-unit recordings under anesthesia. CCI produced rapid, persistent mechanical hypersensitivity. Deformation-based morphometry (DBM) revealed regional volumetric alterations including localized contractions in the IV-V cerebellar lobules. Spontaneous LFPs showed reduced absolute δ/θ power, with unchanged relative (normalized) power, while β/γ were unchanged. Multi-unit activity in CCI mice exhibited higher firing rates, shorter inter-spike intervals, and larger spike amplitudes. Peripheral stimulation evoked larger responses in CCI. Neuropathic pain is associated with structural remodeling, suppressed spontaneous slow-band cerebellar activity and enhanced unit/evoked responsiveness, which we interpret, as a working hypothesis, as a low-synchrony/high-gain operating regime. These structural and electrophysiological changes are candidate signatures that motivate future mechanistic and causal studies of cerebellar involvement in neuropathic pain.

title: Trajectory of influencing factors for post-thrombolysis early neurological deterioration and long-term functional recovery: insights from parallel explainable machine learning models.
abstract: Ischemic brain injury after intravenous thrombolysis (IVT) produces highly variable early deterioration and later disability, yet most prognostic models treat risk as a static, admission-only construct. This leaves the temporal reorganization of influencing factors poorly defined. In 609 consecutive patients treated with IVT alone within 4.5 h of last known well, we built three parallel explainable machine-learning models for 24-hour early neurological deterioration (END), poor function at 1 week, and poor function at 3 months. Stage-specific predictor sets followed the information actually available at each decision point, while an identical analytical pipeline (multi-method feature selection, Bayesian optimization, and synthetic minority oversampling) kept the comparisons methodologically aligned. Cross-validated areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve were 0.742, 0.831 and 0.914. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analysis showed a coherent trajectory after ischemic injury: metabolic load and early infarct burden (Alberta Stroke Program Early CT Score) dominated the hyperacute window; baseline National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale score and intracranial hemorrhage rose in the subacute window; discharge disposition, age and large-vessel occlusion dominated chronic outcome. A glucose × stroke-severity interaction further indicated that metabolic stress is not uniform across severity strata. These results provide a computational description of how clinically measurable factors re-weight over time after reperfusion, and they support phase-specific management of post-ischemic recovery.

title: Methylphenidate-associated brain structural changes and neuroimaging predictors of treatment response in youth with ADHD: a systematic review.
abstract: Background Methylphenidate (MPH) is a psychostimulant widely prescribed to children with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). Although its clinical efficacy is well established, its lasting effects on the developing brain remain unclear. Objective This systematic review aimed to examine associations between long-term MPH treatment and brain structure in children and adolescents with ADHD using structural magnetic resonance imaging (sMRI) and diffusion tensor imaging (DTI), distinguishing longitudinal treatment-effect studies from cross-sectional medication-history comparisons and baseline neuroimaging predictors of treatment response. Methods A systematic search was conducted in MEDLINE and Embase databases. Studies were included if they investigated structural brain changes (gray matter volume, white matter integrity and cortical thickness) after at least four weeks of MPH treatment in children with ADHD. Data extraction and quality assessment were performed using the NIH quality assessment tool. Results Eight studies met the inclusion criteria: three longitudinal studies using repeated MRI to assess within-subject treatment effects, two cross-sectional comparisons based on medication history, and three studies using baseline neuroimaging to predict subsequent treatment response. Greater putamen volume was associated with medication status ad volume with better treatment response in the cross-sectional and predictive analyses, while cortical effects were less consistent and mainly age-dependent in frontal areas. White matter findings were subtle and inconsistent across studies, and cortical thickness evidence-limited to one study-suggests short-term, possibly transient effects in children. originalAbstract:
Background

Methylphenidate (MPH) is a psychostimulant widely prescribed to children with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). Although its clinical efficacy is well established, its lasting effects on the developing brain remain unclear.

Objective

This systematic review aimed to examine associations between long-term MPH treatment and brain structure in children and adolescents with ADHD using structural magnetic resonance imaging (sMRI) and diffusion tensor imaging (DTI), distinguishing longitudinal treatment-effect studies from cross-sectional medication-history comparisons and baseline neuroimaging predictors of treatment response.

Methods

A systematic search was conducted in MEDLINE and Embase databases. Studies were included if they investigated structural brain changes (gray matter volume, white matter integrity and cortical thickness) after at least four weeks of MPH treatment in children with ADHD. Data extraction and quality assessment were performed using the NIH quality assessment tool.

Results

Eight studies met the inclusion criteria: three longitudinal studies using repeated MRI to assess within-subject treatment effects, two cross-sectional comparisons based on medication history, and three studies using baseline neuroimaging to predict subsequent treatment response. Greater putamen volume was associated with medication status ad volume with better treatment response in the cross-sectional and predictive analyses, while cortical effects were less consistent and mainly age-dependent in frontal areas. White matter findings were subtle and inconsistent across studies, and cortical thickness evidence-limited to one study-suggests short-term, possibly transient effects in children.

Conclusion

MPH treatment is associated l with age-dependent differences in brain structure in children and adolescents with ADHD; however, the limited number of included studies varied substantially in design, (cross-sectional and predictive studies alongside longitudinal treatment-effect studies), methodology, and reported outcomes, making firm causal conclusions difficult. Future research should prioritize larger, standardized, long-term longitudinal studies that account for developmental factors.

title: Multisystem assessment of white matter tracts in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis using NODDI and TractSeg.
abstract: Background Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a multisystem neurodegenerative disorder affecting motor, cognitive, and sensory networks. Conventional diffusion MRI lacks specificity for complex white matter pathology. This study combined neurite orientation dispersion and density imaging (NODDI) with automated fiber segmentation (TractSeg) to systematically evaluate microstructural alterations across multiple white matter pathways in a single ALS cohort. Methods We combined NODDI with automated TractSeg fiber segmentation in 83 sporadic ALS patients and 59 healthy controls. NODDI metrics (NDI, ODI, ISOVF) were extracted from 98 nodes along 19 tracts. Group comparisons used ANCOVA with FDR correction (q < 0.05). Results The left corticospinal tract (CST) showed ODI elevation and NDI reduction, and the right CST showed more extensive injury with ODI elevation, widespread NDI reduction, and ISOVF elevation. The corpus callosum exhibited focal changes in the rostral body, the anterior midbody and the posterior midbody involving ODI, NDI, and ISOVF. Among cerebellar motor, visuospatial processing, and limbic pathways, only the right superior longitudinal fasciculus II showed ISOVF elevation. Visual and language pathways predominantly showed ISOVF elevation, with additional NDI elevation in the right optic radiation and left arcuate fasciculus. Conclusions This study demonstrates asymmetric, pathway-selective white matter pathology in ALS. Focal damage in the mid-body of the corpus callosum supports its role as a hub for interhemispheric disease propagation. Evidence of both degeneration and possible compensatory neurite reorganization in visual and language pathways further establishes ALS as a multisystem network disorder. NODDI combined with TractSeg offers biologically specific imaging biomarkers for disease monitoring and clinical subtyping.

title: In vivo probabilistic atlas mapping reveals brainstem nuclei volume increases in idiopathic REM sleep behavior disorder.
abstract: Objective Idiopathic rapid eye movement sleep behavior disorder (iRBD) serves as a key prodromal marker of synucleinopathies, and its core symptoms are closely associated with brainstem pathology. Nevertheless, in vivo imaging research on brainstem nuclei in iRBD patients is still limited due to methodological constraints. This study aimed to explore volume changes of brainstem nuclei in iRBD patients via a fine-grained probabilistic atlas, and analyze their clinical correlations and diagnostic value. Methods We enrolled 3D T1-weighted MRI data of 178 iRBD patients and 111 healthy controls from the PPMI database. After preprocessing, 54 brainstem nuclei were segmented using the Brainstem Navigator atlas, and their relative volumes were compared between groups with multiple comparison correction. Correlation analyses with clinical scales and ROC analyses were conducted for nuclei with significant inter-group differences. Results Compared to HCs, iRBD patients presented significantly enlarged relative volumes in the left cuneiform nucleus, left lateral parabrachial nucleus, and left superior medullary reticular formation. The volumes of the latter two nuclei were positively correlated with RBDSQ scores and related to autonomic, affective and cognitive indicators. The AUC of single nucleus for iRBD diagnosis ranged from 0.607 to 0.637, while the combined model reached 0.674. Conclusion These findings confirm volumetric enlargement in specific brainstem nuclei of iRBD patients, suggesting early pathological remodeling in these regions. They clarify the brainstem structural basis of iRBD symptoms and suggest that brainstem nuclei volumes, with moderate discriminative performance, may serve as supplementary imaging markers to complement clinical assessments in iRBD.
