title: Multicenter evaluation of total body irradiation planning strategies: A DGMP working group study on large-field irradiation techniques.
abstract: Purpose Total body irradiation (TBI) is an integral component of conditioning regimens for hematopoietic stem cell transplantation. Despite similar biological objectives, planning and delivery of TBI vary substantially across institutions. The aim of this study was to quantitatively assess inter-institutional and technique-dependent variability in contemporary TBI planning by comparing dose distributions generated under standardized conditions across multiple centers in Germany and Switzerland. Methods Twenty-four radiotherapy centers received anonymized total-body computed tomography (CT) datasets of a standardized dummy patient in head-first supine and prone orientations, including predefined points of interest (POI) and organs at risk (OARs). Each center was asked to generate TBI plans for two prescription levels (8 Gy in 4 fractions and 12 Gy in 6 fractions) using its local planning standards, with the entire body defined as the planning target volume (PTV). Submissions included treatment-planning-system (TPS)-based 3D dose distributions and in-house table-based calculations. TPS plans were centrally imported into a TPS for extraction of target coverage and OAR dose metrics, while table-based submissions were evaluated using aggregated POI doses. Results In total, 45 TBI treatment plans from 24 centers were analyzed, including 24 plans for 8 Gy and 21 plans for 12 Gy. Both TPS-based and table-based planning approaches were represented across a broad range of clinical techniques, including volumetic modulated arc therapy (VMAT), Tomotherapy, sweeping beam, static field, bilateral, and translation couch setups. Marked inter-institutional variability was observed, particularly for lung, lens, and kidney doses. At the 12 Gy prescription level, mean lung doses differed by more than 3 Gy between centers, corresponding to relative variations of up to approximately 30%. Conformal intensity-modulated techniques (VMAT and Tomotherapy) showed the highest consistency across institutions, whereas non-conformal approaches exhibited substantially larger dose variability. Increased lung sparing at 12 Gy was consistently associated with reduced target coverage compared to 8 Gy. Conclusion This study provides the first standardized multicenter planning-based comparison of contemporary TBI approaches in Germany and Switzerland. By quantifying inter-institutional variability in dose distributions under uniform conditions, the results outline the current heterogeneity of clinical practice and the range of achievable dosimetric outcomes. Rather than defining a reference standard, these findings establish a structured benchmark of existing planning strategies and highlight the need for harmonization, thereby providing a foundation for future consensus development and end-to-end validation efforts.

title: Impact of ROI definition on head and neck cancer FDG-PET radiomics.
abstract: Due to its rising incidence, head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) represents a global health challenge, and risk stratification is important for personalized treatment. 18 F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) positron emission tomography (PET)-derived biomarkers show considerable potential for predicting HNSCC radio(chemo)therapy outcomes. However, the definition of the three-dimensional primary tumor region of interest (ROI) varies, with anatomically defined gross tumor volumes (GTV-ROIs) and PET-based metabolic tumor volumes (MTV-ROIs) often used interchangeably. Therefore, we assessed the effect of these ROI definitions on extracted radiomics features and radio(chemo)therapy outcome predictions in a multicenter dataset of 741 HNSCC patients. Features from the two ROI definitions were compared using the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC). The investigated study endpoints, locoregional control (LRC) and overall survival (OS), were evaluated using the number of outcome-associated features in univariate Cox regression, as well as by the performance of multivariable machine-learning models. GTV-ROIs and MTV-ROIs yielded substantially different radiomics features, with a median ICC of 0.63 (IQR, 0.37-0.85). The MTV-ROIs led to a higher number of OS-associated features (continuous features: p = 0.003, binarized features: p = 0.015) and comparable model C-indexes, 0.61 (95% CI: 0.51-0.69; MTV-ROIs) vs.0.58 (95% CI: 0.49-0.66; GTV-ROIs) for LRC, and 0.65 (95% CI: 0.59-0.71; MTV-ROIs) vs.0.63 (95% CI: 0.56-0.69; GTV-ROIs) for OS. To conclude, the definition of the HNSCC primary tumor ROI has a notable effect on FDG-PET feature values and their prognostic potential, whereas its effect on multivariable model performance appears limited.

title: Activity and safety of first-line pumitamig plus nab-paclitaxel in triple-negative breast cancer: a single-arm, phase 1b/2 trial.
abstract: Background Pumitamig, an investigational bispecific antibody targeting programmed death ligand-1 and vascular endothelial growth factor A, has shown preliminary efficacy across several tumour types. We aimed to evaluate the safety and activity of pumitamig plus nab-paclitaxel as first-line treatment in patients with advanced or metastatic triple-negative breast cancer. Methods In this single-arm, phase 1b/2 trial conducted at ten sites (hospitals and cancer centres) in China, patients aged 18-75 years with histologically documented, unresectable, locally advanced or metastatic triple-negative breast cancer, an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status of 1 or less, and one or more measurable lesion (as per Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumours, version 1.1) received first-line pumitamig (20 mg/kg intravenously once every 2 weeks) plus nab-paclitaxel (100 mg/m 2 intravenously on days 1, 8, and 15 of each 28-day cycle) until disease progression or unacceptable toxicity. In phase 1b, six patients received pumitamig (20 mg/kg once every 2 weeks intravenously plus nab-paclitaxel 100 mg/m 2 intravenously on days 1, 8, and 15 of each 28-day cycle) and were monitored for treatment-emergent adverse events, before subsequent enrolment in phase 2. The primary endpoints were confirmed objective response rate and safety, assessed in the efficacy-evaluable population, defined as all patients who received one or more doses of study drug and had measurable disease at baseline and at least one efficacy assessment. This trial is registered with chictr.org.cn (ChiCTR2200060400) and ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT05918133), and is closed to recruitment. Findings Between June 27, 2022, and March 15, 2023, 42 patients were enrolled, received one or more doses of pumitamig plus nab-paclitaxel (median duration of exposure 9·0 months, 95% CI 6·9-11·7) and had one or more tumour assessments. All patients were Chinese and female; median age was 53 years (IQR 41-60). At a median follow-up of 35·2 months (95% CI 33·0-36·1), the confirmed objective response rate was 73·8% (95% CI 58·0-86·1; 31 of 42 patients), including one complete response and 30 partial responses. The most frequent treatment-related adverse events of grade 3 or worse were decreased neutrophil count (13 [31%] of 42 patients), decreased white blood cell count (11 [26%]), proteinuria (six [14%]), and febrile neutropenia (five [12%]). Nine (21%) patients reported 14 treatment-related serious adverse events (alanine aminotransferase increased n=2; febrile neutropenia n=2; pancreatitis n=2; and ascites, aspartate aminotransferase increased, abdominal distension, γ-glutamyltransferase increased, blood alkaline phosphatase increased, cataract, macular oedema, and retinal vein occlusion all n=1). Treatment-related adverse events led to discontinuation of both nab-paclitaxel and pumitamig in four (10%) patients, discontinuation of nab-paclitaxel only in three (7%) patients, and discontinuation of pumitamig only in two (5%) patients. There were no treatment-related deaths. Interpretation Treatment with first-line pumitamig plus nab-paclitaxel showed encouraging antitumour activity in patients with advanced or metastatic triple-negative breast cancer and a safety profile consistent with the mode of actions of both agents. These findings warrant further clinical evaluation in global phase 2 and 3 trials. Funding Biotheus (BioNTech group). title: Cancer in the Commonwealth: a Lancet Oncology Commission.
abstract: Cancer is now one of the defining health and development challenges of our time. The 56 nations of the Commonwealth, home to 2·7 billion people, mirror this global burden. Recorded cancer cases across member states rose by 35% in 2008-18 and the number of deaths reached almost 1·7 million in 2018. The Lancet Oncology Commission on cancer in the Commonwealth was convened to ask a deceptively simple question: how can 56 diverse nations act collectively to close the widening gap between the burden of cancer and the capacity of each country to respond? 80 researchers, clinicians, policy makers, and civil society members, organised into five working groups and ten research streams, spent 2 years assembling the evidence base for this report. Using a validated microsimulation model, we estimate that 5-year net survival across eleven common cancers in the Commonwealth stood at just 30·7% in 2020, ranging from 4·1% in low-income countries (LICs) to 59·0% in high-income countries (HICs), driven overwhelmingly by late-stage presentation, which affects 62% of patients in LICs compared with 43% in HICs. This difference in survival is compounded by chronic underinvestment. Infrastructure gaps are equally stark: only 12% of countries meet international benchmarks for CT imaging, 22% for hospital density, and 40% for radiotherapy. Governance is underdeveloped too: barely one-third of Commonwealth countries have a national cancer control plan meeting basic quality criteria. Research investment also mirrors these inequities: between 2016 and 2023, Commonwealth countries collectively invested only US$165 per cancer-related disability adjusted life year. Yet the case for investment is unambiguous. Our modelling shows that a comprehensive scaleup of treatment, imaging, and quality of care could raise 5-year net survival across the Commonwealth from 30·7% to 52·9%, averting an estimated 5·8 million deaths and adding 113 million life-years between 2025 and 2035, at an incremental cost of $36·7 billion, delivering a return of between four and twenty dollars on every dollar invested. Crucially, this investment need not depend chiefly on external aid, which is contracting sharply at present. Our modelling for 38 low-income and middle-income Commonwealth countries suggests that up to $701 billion in additional domestic fiscal space could be mobilised between 2025 and 2030, through budget reprioritisation, macroeconomic growth, targeted taxation, and prudent borrowing. On this evidence, the Commission proposes six priority actions. These commitments are ambitious, set against an unusually turbulent geopolitical backdrop of declining official development assistance, fiscal retrenchment, and contested multilateralism. Yet it is precisely this backdrop that gives the Commonwealth its distinctive advantage: a voluntary association spanning every income level and continent, bound by common legal and regulatory traditions, capable of collective action that neither purely bilateral aid nor multilateral institutions under strain can easily replicate.

title: Contralateral tonsillectomy in oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma: diagnostic yield and procedural burden.
abstract: Objective Unilateral radiotherapy for well-lateralised oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma reduces treatment toxicity. This study evaluated whether routine contralateral tonsillectomy, performed to look for synchronous tonsillar malignancies, is justified. Methods A retrospective analysis was conducted of 81 patients treated with curative intent for oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma at a tertiary centre (2022-2024). All patients underwent positron emission tomography computed tomography. Contralateral tonsillectomy was performed in candidates for unilateral radiotherapy. Results Forty-two patients underwent contralateral tonsillectomy. Synchronous contralateral squamous cell carcinoma was identified in one patient (2.4 per cent) who required bilateral cervical chemoradiation because of extranodal extension found on neck dissection. Eleven patients (26 per cent) underwent staged procedures after a median interval of 21 days. Post-tonsillectomy haemorrhage requiring hospital re-admission occurred in one patient (2.4 per cent). Conclusion Routine contralateral tonsillectomy did not yield any findings that altered the laterality of treatment in any patient. This suggests that omitting contralateral tonsillectomy may complement de-escalation strategies.

title: Pericarditis in COVID-19: a focus on the paediatric population.
abstract: Background COVID-19, caused by SARS-CoV-2, is primarily a respiratory illness but may cause cardiovascular complications, including pericarditis. Pediatric SARS-CoV-2-associated pericarditis remains uncommon and likely underreported. This review summarizes the epidemiology, pathophysiology, clinical presentation, diagnosis, management, and outcomes of pericarditis associated with SARS-CoV-2 infection in children. Methods We narratively reviewed the available literature on SARS-CoV-2-associated pericarditis in the pediatric population, including isolated acute pericarditis, myopericarditis, pericardial effusion, cardiac tamponade, and pericardial involvement in multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children (MIS-C). Results The true incidence of pediatric SARS-CoV-2-associated pericarditis remains unclear. Reported cases suggest that older children and adolescents are more commonly affected, typically presenting with chest pain, fever, dyspnea, or tachycardia, whereas younger children may exhibit nonspecific symptoms. Diagnosis relies on clinical criteria supported by electrocardiography, echocardiography, inflammatory markers, and cardiac biomarkers, with cardiac magnetic resonance imaging useful when myocardial involvement is suspected. Available evidence suggests a predominantly immune-mediated pathophysiology involving cytokine dysregulation and systemic inflammation, with limited evidence of direct viral invasion. Management is largely extrapolated from established pediatric pericarditis principles and adult data. Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and colchicine are first-line therapies, while corticosteroids or intravenous immunoglobulin may be considered in selected inflammatory or MIS-C-associated cases, and interleukin-1 blockade in refractory or recurrent disease. Most affected children recover, although severe pericardial effusion, tamponade, and recurrence have been reported. Conclusion Pediatric SARS-CoV-2-associated pericarditis encompasses a spectrum of clinical presentations and generally carries a favorable prognosis. Nevertheless, potentially serious complications emphasize the importance of early recognition, differentiation from myocarditis and MIS-C, and structured follow-up.

title: Band-Pass Fluorescence Activation via Dual-Responsive Molecular Design in the NIR-II Window for In Vivo pH Sensing.
abstract: Real-time monitoring of physiological pH in living systems is essential for accurate disease evaluation and therapeutic guidance. However, conventional pH-responsive probes typically operate through monotonic activation and lack window selectivity, limiting their capacity to report further microenvironmental changes after crossing the activation threshold. Here, we report a NIR-II molecularly engineered band-pass pH (BPpH) sensing strategy that exhibits a non-monotonic "off-on-off" fluorescence response. By integrating an acid-responsive spirolactam switch with an alkaline-sensitive phenolic regulator, the BPpH probes enable window-restricted signal output within a defined pH range. BPpH-3 displays fluorescence activation from pH 3.6 to 5.2 and deactivation from pH 5.2 to 8.0, affording dual apparent pKa values of 4.16 and 7.42 and establishing a response window. Unlike conventional monotonic turn-on probes, this band-pass response enables continuous tracking of pH changes across the therapeutic process, and BPpH-3 further enables dynamic evaluation of therapeutic efficacy in a skin inflammation model, allowing timely assessment of treatment progression and dosing sufficiency. Moreover, its window-constrained response mitigates signal over-amplification under extreme acidification, facilitating improved tumor margin delineation for precision resection under NIR-II imaging guidance. The band-pass sensing strategy presented here provides a transferable framework for window-regulated detection of diverse physiological parameters and holds promise for integration with multiple diagnostic imaging modalities.

title: An Enzyme-Triggered Self-Immobilizing Dual-Modal Probe for Precision Imaging and Sustained Gas Therapy of Early-Stage MASH.
abstract: The clinical management of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) is hindered by the lack of noninvasive molecular diagnostics and effective targeted therapies. Although hydrogen sulfide (H2S) can ameliorate MASH via antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects, conventional H2S donors suffer from uncontrolled burst release and rapid in vivo clearance. Here, we report AzoR-Cy-Gd, a magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)/fluorescence imaging (FLI)-guided H2S theranostic platform for early diagnosis, severity assessment, and visualized intervention of MASH. This hypoxia-responsive theranostic probe, featuring a reductively cleavable azo linkage, integrates a near-infrared cyanine fluorophore, a Gd-DO3A MRI contrast unit, and a carbonyl sulfide (COS)/H2S-releasing module. In MASH lesions, hypoxia-associated reductive activation induces cleavage of the azo bond, which subsequently triggers a self-immolative cascade, generating quinone methide (QM) for in situ protein anchoring and releasing COS for carbonic anhydrase-mediated H2S production. This synchronized activation restores intramolecular charge transfer, producing a 50-fold fluorescence enhancement and increasing relaxivity (r1) from 8.9 to 14.1 mM-1 s-1 while prolonging lesion retention. In a methionine/choline-deficient diet-induced mouse model, AzoR-Cy-Gd sensitively visualized hepatic pathogenesis and tracked disease progression from 4 to 8 weeks. Moreover, localized H2S release effectively suppressed inflammation, reduced lipid accumulation, and restored liver architecture and function. Overall, AzoR-Cy-Gd establishes a self-reporting "see-and-treat" strategy for precision MASH theranostics.

title: Acid-Catalyzed Synthesis of Octacosanyl Fatty Acid Esters and Their In Vivo Biological Activities.
abstract: Octacosanol (C28), mainly found in rice bran and sugar cane, possesses cholesterol-lowering properties but is limited by poor bioavailability. This study optimized the sulfuric acid-catalyzed synthesis of lauric acid-esterified octacosanol (LEO) and oleic acid-esterified octacosanol (OEO) to enhance their bioactivity. Under optimized conditions (140-150 °C for 3 h), esterification rates reached 97.8% for LEO and 90.6% for OEO, with structures confirmed via gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS), nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR), and Fourier transform infrared spectrometer (FTIR). In high-fat diet-induced obese C57BL/6J mice, both esters significantly improved serum lipid profiles compared to nonesterified octacosanol, with OEO showing the strongest efficacy in reducing total cholesterol and elevating HDL-c. Furthermore, a 28-day subacute toxicological assessment in ICR mice revealed no clinical, biochemical, or hematological abnormalities, indicating a favorable preliminary safety profile for OEO. These results suggest that OEO is a promising functional ingredient for mitigating hyperlipidemia and cardiovascular disease risk, offering improved application potential in dietary supplements.

title: Evaluation and an Exploratory Human Study of 99mTc-Labeled PSMA-Targeting Agents with Reduced Renal Uptake via Proline Incorporation.
abstract: Excessive renal uptake of prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA)-targeted radiopharmaceuticals remains a major challenge in prostate cancer (PCa) detection and therapy. We developed 99mTc-labeled PSMA radioligands incorporating d- or l-proline as a conformationally constrained linker combined with optimized co-ligands to reduce kidney accumulation. The resulting hydrophilic complexes achieved high radiochemical yields and strong in vitro stability. The optimal radiotracer, [99mTc]Tc-L-M1, exhibited high LNCaP (PSMA++) cell affinity (Kd = 19.09 nM) and the lowest kidney uptake (6.50 ± 0.32% ID/g, Kunming mice, 2 h p.i.). It accumulated effectively in both LNCaP (PSMA++) and 22Rv1 (PSMA+) tumors with excellent target-to-nontarget ratios and strong PSMA specificity. SPECT/CT imaging confirmed low renal accumulation, consistent with biodistribution data. Preliminary clinical trials demonstrated clear delineation of small PCa lesions, highlighting [99mTc]Tc-L-M1 as a promising PSMA-specific radiotracer with reduced kidney uptake for clinical application.

title: Development and Preclinical Evaluation of [68Ga]Ga-DOTA-L3: A Novel PET Tracer for Quantitative Imaging of Carbonic Anhydrase IX.
abstract: Carbonic anhydrase IX (CA IX) is a key biomarker for tumor hypoxia and a promising target for molecular imaging. In this study, we developed [68Ga]Ga-DOTA-L3, a novel small-molecule CA IX-targeted PET tracer. The radiolabeling was optimized to consistently achieve a radiochemical purity of >98% (10 μg precursor, 90 °C, pH 4.5, 10 min), with excellent stability in saline and FBS up to 240 min. In vivo studies demonstrated rapid blood clearance and predominant renal excretion. Surface plasmon resonance analysis demonstrated high-affinity binding of the DOTA-L3 precursor toward CA IX (Kd = 7.60 ± 0.37 nM) with highest affinity observed for CA IX among the tested isoforms. MicroPET/CT imaging (30-240 min p.i.) showed robust tumor accumulation in OSRC-2 (SUVmean = 1.47 ± 0.21) and HT-29 (SUVmean = 1.03 ± 0.12) xenografts, while minimal uptake was observed in CA IX-low FTC-238 tumors (SUVmean = 0.21 ± 0.05) at 60 min p.i. PET-derived tumor uptake showed a strong linear correlation with CA IX expression levels (R2 = 0.976, P < 0.001) across the three tumor models. High tumor-to-muscle and tumor-to-blood ratios further confirm favorable imaging contrast (T/M = 27.53 ± 1.89 and T/B = 24.61 ± 2.35 at 240 min p.i. for OSRC-2 model). These results support [68Ga]Ga-DOTA-L3 as a promising candidate for non-invasive assessment of CA IX-associated hypoxia and as a scaffold for future theranostic development.

title: Vitamin D deficiency, quantitative ultrasound parameters and bone biomarkers in adolescents.
abstract: Background Vitamin D is crucial for bone mineralization and skeletal growth during adolescence; nevertheless, deficiency remains widespread even in sun-rich regions. This study examined serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D [25(OH)D] levels and their associations with bone status and turnover markers in Mexican adolescents. Methods A cross-sectional analysis was performed on 914 participants aged 11-18 years residing in Tlaxcala, Mexico. Anthropometric, socioeconomic, and biochemical data were collected, including 25(OH)D, parathyroid hormone (PTH), fibroblast growth factor 23 (FGF23), osteocalcin (OC), osteopontin (OPN), osteoprotegerin (OPG), and RANKL. Bone status was assessed using quantitative ultrasound (QUS) at the radius and tibia. Results The median 25(OH)D concentration was 19.8 ng/mL; 44.3% of adolescents were categorized as having insufficiency, and 50.4% as having deficiency. Girls showed significantly lower levels than boys (18.5 vs. 22.1 ng/mL, p < 0.0001) and a higher prevalence of deficiency (62% vs. 36%). Low bone mineral density (LBDM; Score Z ≤ -1) occurred in 18.7% at the radius and 24.3% at the tibia. Serum 25(OH)D was positively associated with OC (β = 0.28, p = 0.013) and OPN (β = 0.28, p = 0.034) and inversely with OPG (β = -1.86, p = 0.050), particularly among girls, while no associations were found with PTH, FGF23, RANKL, or QUS parameters. Conclusion These findings reveal widespread vitamin D deficiency and sex-specific alterations in bone remodeling, highlighting the need for early prevention strategies tailored to vulnerable adolescents. Impact Vitamin D deficiency is highly prevalent among adolescents in central Mexico, especially girls, despite abundant sunlight. In a large pediatric cohort, this study links serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D with bone turnover biomarkers and quantitative ultrasound measures, showing sex-specific associations with markers of bone formation and remodeling. These findings suggest that inadequate vitamin D may alter bone metabolism before detectable reductions in bone density occur, supporting early screening and targeted interventions for youth living under similar environmental and socioeconomic conditions.

title: Comparing MRI-based scoring systems for neuroprognostication in neonatal encephalopathy.
abstract: Background Neonatal encephalopathy (NE) remains a significant cause of neurodevelopmental impairment. However, which MRI-based scoring system best predicts 36-month outcomes remains unclear. Methods A prospective cohort of 102 neonates ≥36 weeks gestation with NE underwent early postnatal brain MRI. Images were scored using five established systems: Barkovich, Weeke, Trivedi, Rutherford, and NICHD-NRN. Neurodevelopmental outcomes were evaluated at 36 months. Prognostic performance was analyzed using logistic regression and receiver operating characteristic curves. The best predictive model was determined using pairwise correlation to reduce highly correlated variables, and then backward selection to optimize the linear regression model. Results The Weeke total score showed the highest predictive accuracy for Bayley Scales of Infant Development motor outcomes (AUC 0.7647). The Weeke gray matter subscore was most predictive of Child Behavior Checklist internalizing problems (AUC 0.7735). No scoring system reliably predicted cognitive, language, or externalizing problems (AUC < 0.7). The optimal motor outcomes prediction model included 5 Weeke variables: basal ganglia, posterior limb of internal capsule, perirolandic cortex, cerebellar hemorrhage location, and basal ganglia lactate. Conclusions MRI-based scoring systems have limited prognostic value beyond motor outcomes after NE. The Weeke score offers the most reliable motor prediction, achievable using only five parameters. Impact Existing MRI scoring systems have limited prognostic value beyond motor outcomes after neonatal encephalopathy. The Weeke score offers the most reliable motor prediction. Only 5 Weeke scoring system variables are needed to optimize motor prediction. Deep gray matter injury is associated with internalizing behavioral outcomes. A simplified, user-friendly prognostic model can support accurate outcome prediction by a broader range of clinicians.

title: MRI measures of oxygen extraction fraction in the subacute phase of mild neonatal hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy.
abstract: Background Early identification of newborns with mild encephalopathy at risk of clinical progression is critical. Our group has previously demonstrated regional quantification of oxygen extraction fraction (OEF), a noninvasive MRI-derived measure of cerebral oxygen utilization in newborns with encephalopathy receiving therapeutic hypothermia (TH). This study evaluates whether regional OEF measured between 2 and 7 days of life distinguishes newborns with mild encephalopathy who are not treated with TH and subsequently exhibit clinical progression within the first day of life from those who remain clinically stable. Methods Vessel-specific OEF maps of the brain were obtained using the accelerated T 2 -relaxation-under-phase-contrast (aTRUPC) MRI technique from full-term newborns with mild encephalopathy and healthy controls. OEF was quantified across six predefined venous drainage regions. Results Fifty-three full-term newborns (28 with mild encephalopathy, 25 healthy controls) were enrolled. Seven newborns with mild encephalopathy showed clinical progression on the first day of life and received TH (TH group); the remaining did not receive TH (non-TH group). OEF was significantly lower in cortical regions in the TH group compared with healthy controls and the non-TH group. Conclusion Cortical OEF represents an innovative imaging biomarker. Prospective studies are needed to determine its value for risk stratification during the therapeutic window. Impact Early identification of newborns with mild encephalopathy at risk of progression remains challenging during the therapeutic window. Cortical oxygen extraction fraction (OEF) measured between 2 and 7 days of life was significantly lower in newborns who progressed within the first day of life than in newborns with mild encephalopathy who did not progress and healthy controls. Regional OEF may provide a noninvasive biomarker for early risk stratification and treatment decision-making in newborns with mild encephalopathy.

title: Magnetic resonance imaging of congenital brain malformations.
abstract: Congenital brain malformations can contribute to significant morbidity and mortality. Severity and prognosis depend on the character, extent, and anatomical localization as well as associated genetic syndromes and other organ system involvement. Correct diagnosis is crucial for early interventions including supportive therapies, prognostic and genetic counseling, medical management, and/or surgical correction. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) improves early diagnosis and prognostication. This review outlines clinical signs and symptoms that may warrant an MRI followed by an overview of various cerebral, posterior fossa, and vascular malformations, as well as corpus callosum abnormalities with representative MR images as well as recommendations on how to set up and optimally perform MRI. Lastly, this review presents perspectives and focus areas for further research. IMPACT: What is the key message of your article? Magnetic resonance imaging is a key component to the diagnosis and prognosis of congenital brain malformations. What does it add to the existing literature? This review provides an updated review on the current literature on congenital brain malformations as well as recommendations for integrating MRI into clinical practice. What is the impact? This review contributes with recommendations on what to expect when interpreting MR images of neonates with suspected congenital brain malformations.

title: Anatomy of periprostatic nerves and nerve-sparing strategy for radical prostatectomy.
abstract: Background Radical prostatectomy is an important curative treatment for localized prostate cancer, but postoperative urinary incontinence and erectile dysfunction substantially impair quality of life. Understanding individual variation in periprostatic nerves, fascia, and supporting structures is essential for balancing oncological control with functional preservation. This narrative review examines periprostatic nerve and fascial anatomy, nerve-sparing grading systems, established surgical techniques, and emerging adjuncts for individualized surgical planning. Methods PubMed was searched through July 2026 using 'prostate', 'pelvic autonomic nerve', 'neurovascular bundle', 'nerve sparing', 'radical prostatectomy', 'continence', 'erectile function', and 'NeuroSAFE'. Relevant guidelines and standard anatomical texts were also reviewed, alongside anatomical and clinical studies directly addressing periprostatic nerve anatomy, nerve-sparing techniques, or functional and oncological outcomes. Results Anatomical and histological studies show substantial variation in periprostatic nerve distribution. Nerve fibres are not confined to conventional posterolateral neurovascular bundles. Some extend into the anterolateral prostate and course through multilayered, heterogeneous fascial structures. Anatomy-based grading systems provide practical intraoperative frameworks but cannot accurately quantify nerve preservation in individual patients. Bilateral or more extensive nerve sparing is associated with better recovery of urinary continence and erectile function. However, these associations are influenced by baseline function, tumour risk, surgeon experience, and inconsistent outcome definitions. Contemporary approaches increasingly preserve a broader complex of nerves, fascia, and supporting structures. Refined techniques may improve early functional recovery, although comparative long-term evidence remains limited. Multiparametric magnetic resonance imaging, NeuroSAFE, and intraoperative nerve-identification technologies may further support individualized planning and real-time adjustment of dissection planes. Conclusions A detailed understanding of individualized periprostatic nerve and fascial anatomy underpins effective nerve-sparing surgery. Integrating anatomy-based grading, patient-specific planning, and advanced adjunctive technologies may improve the balance between oncological control and functional preservation.

title: Multi-omics, spatial omics and artificial intelligence in chronic diseases: current applications and future directions.
abstract: Chronic diseases exhibit multiscale heterogeneity and spatial organization, yet analytical frameworks often fail to connect molecular perturbations, tissue architecture, and clinical outcomes within a unified evidence framework. Bulk and single-modality approaches can identify regulatory or cellular alterations but provide limited insight into why pathogenic programs emerge in anatomical regions, how they shape disease niches, and how they drive divergent clinical trajectories. Multi-omics partially addresses this gap by resolving interconnected layers of regulation, transcription, protein activity, and metabolism, whereas spatial omics maps these processes within preserved tissue architecture, enabling the delineation of lesion topology, interface states, and multicellular microenvironments. Artificial intelligence (AI) may further extend this framework by integrating molecular, spatial, imaging, and clinical data into disease representations that support disease stratification, the discovery of mechanistic patterns, and clinically testable predictions, provided that models are externally validated, biologically interpretable, and robust to dataset bias and domain shift. In this review, we examine how multi-omics, spatial omics, and AI can bridge the disconnect between molecular profiling, spatial pathology, and clinical translation in chronic disease research. We discuss six representative disease domains before synthesizing insights into how these approaches define molecular endotypes, map pathological niches, identify recurrent mechanistic patterns, and generate interpretable surrogate readouts for diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment stratification. We also highlight limitations, including preanalytical variability, inconsistencies across platforms, limited external generalizability, and the challenges of translating high-dimensional outputs into deployable clinical tools. Finally, we outline priorities for scalable evidence systems, mechanism-guided validation frameworks, multimodal model interpretability, and prospective clinical implementation.

title: Distribution patterns and temporal detection profiles of MRI-visible tract-specific wallerian degeneration after traumatic cervical spinal cord injury.
abstract: Study design Retrospective study. Objectives To characterize the distribution patterns, associated clinical factors, and temporal detection profiles of tract-specific MRI-visible Wallerian degeneration (WD) in patients with traumatic cervical spinal cord injury (tCSCI). Setting China Rehabilitation Research Center, Beijing, China. Methods Medical records of patients with tCSCI admitted between January 2015 and December 2024 were reviewed. Primary analyses used the first eligible post-injury MRI. WD was identified on T2-weighted MRI as tract-specific hyperintensity remote from the injury epicenter. Univariable and multivariable logistic regression analyses were performed for dorsal column WD (DC-WD), spinothalamic tract WD (ST-WD), and corticospinal tract WD (CS-WD). Temporal detectability was assessed across five injury-to-MRI interval categories. Results Of 238 patients, DC-WD was detected in 122 (51.3%), ST-WD in 103 (43.3%), and CS-WD in 64 (26.9%). ST-WD occurred only with DC-WD, and CS-WD only with concurrent DC-WD and ST-WD, forming a nested pattern of MRI-visible tract involvement. After multivariable adjustment, the log-transformed injury-to-MRI interval was significantly associated with all three WD subtypes (DC-WD: aOR = 12.74; ST-WD: aOR = 7.96; CS-WD: aOR = 6.45; all p < 0.001). The model-estimated injury-to-MRI intervals corresponding to a 50% predicted probability of MRI-visible WD were 59.1 days for DC-WD, 79.1 days for ST-WD, and 152.9 days for CS-WD. Conclusions Tract-specific MRI-visible WD after tCSCI showed a nested distribution and interval-dependent detectability. These exploratory, cross-sectional estimates should not be interpreted as longitudinal detection times but may provide reference data for MRI interpretation after tCSCI.

title: Radiographic appearance of proximal resin composite restorations bonded with a radiopaque or radiolucent universal adhesive: a randomized clinical trial.
abstract: Objectives This trial evaluated the radiographic appearance of resin composite restorations bonded with a radiopaque universal adhesive compared with a radiolucent universal adhesive, assessed by digital radiography based on modified USPHS criteria. Materials and methods Seventy-four participants with class II cavities were randomly assigned to two groups (n = 37). The intervention group received radiopaque universal adhesive (Scotchbond Universal Plus, 3M ESPE, St. Paul, USA), while the control group received radiolucent universal adhesive (Single Bond Universal adhesive, 3M ESPE, St. Paul, USA). Selective enamel etching was performed, followed by adhesive application and restoration with nanofilled resin composite (Filtek Z350XT, 3M ESPE, St. Paul, USA). Postoperative periapical radiographs were used to evaluate the appearance of the tooth-restoration interface according to modified USPHS criteria, classifying restorations as Alpha (absence of radiolucent line) or Bravo (presence of radiolucent line). Categorical data were analyzed using Fisher's exact test. Absolute risk reduction (risk difference) with 95% confidence interval was calculated to estimate the difference in the risk of detecting a radiolucent adhesive line between the two groups. Results A statistically significant difference was observed between the two groups (P = 0.025). Restorations bonded with the radiopaque adhesive demonstrated a 16.2% absolute reduction in the risk of exhibiting a radiolucent line at the tooth-restoration interface compared with those bonded using the radiolucent adhesive (95% CI: 3.71-28.73%). Conclusions The radiopaque universal adhesive resulted in significantly fewer restorations with visible radiolucent lines at the tooth-restoration interface immediately after restoration placement and may facilitate radiographic interpretation of proximal resin composite restorations. Trial registration https://clinicaltrials.gov/ , (NCT05907928).

title: Automated retinal layer thickness segmentation in neovascular age-related macular degeneration: a comparison of two algorithms.
abstract: Purpose To evaluate the consistency of retinal measurements provided by two automated segmentation algorithms in eyes with neovascular age-related macular degeneration (AMD). Design Retrospective cohort study. Participants Fifty patients with neovascular AMD. Methods Retinal thickness was measured using a Heidelberg Spectralis HRA + OCT spectral-domain device. Measurements were automatically averaged across ETDRS grid subfields centered on the fovea using both the Spectralis built-in software (version 1.10.4.0) and the Orion automated OCT segmentation software (Voxeleron, version 3.0.0). Main outcome measures Differences in quantitative retinal thickness metrics between the two algorithms. Results For inner retinal thickness, the mean difference was 8.97 μm in the central fovea (R² = 0.32), with larger variability in the inner (22.09-28.73 μm; R² = 0.32-0.80) and outer circles (16.02-29.50 μm; R² = 0.45-0.41). Outer retinal thickness showed smaller differences, with a mean of 21.51 μm in the central fovea (R² = 0.36) and modest variation across subfields. The neurosensory retina demonstrated a mean difference of 0.13 μm centrally (R² = 0.66), increasing across ETDRS subfields, with an overall mean difference of 45.30μm (R² = 0.82). Total retinal thickness differed by 43.54 μm centrally (R² = 0.61), with smaller differences across the grid (mean 18.16 μm; R² = 0.60). Conclusions While correlations between the two segmentation algorithms were moderate to strong for several metrics, clinically meaningful mean differences were observed in specific compartments, most notably for central neurosensory and total retinal thickness. These findings indicate that the two algorithms should not be used interchangeably.

title: [ 18 F]FET PET enables histopathology-validated detection of non-contrast-enhancing glioblastoma.
abstract: Accurate visualization of glioblastoma is essential for guiding biopsy, resection and radiotherapy. Contrast-enhanced MRI is routine in clinical practice, yet it can miss metabolically active tumor outside areas of blood-brain barrier disruption. In a histopathology-validated cohort with 472 tissue samples of 61 patients with IDH-wildtype glioblastoma, we show that O-(2-[¹⁸F]fluoroethyl)-L-tyrosine PET ([ 18 F]FET PET) depicts tumor tissue significantly better than contrast-enhanced MRI (CE-MRI), especially in regions that show no enhancement on MRI. [ 18 F]FET PET achieves substantially higher sensitivity for tumor detection (91.2% vs 52.6%) and maintains high reliability in non-enhancing tissue (positive predictive value 98.3%), findings that are consistent across newly diagnosed and recurrent disease and in both cohorts undergoing either resection or biopsy. These results indicate that [ 18 F]FET PET complements MRI by revealing MRI-occult tumor burden. Incorporating amino acid PET into routine planning may therefore improve the accuracy of tumor visualization and, ultimately, patient management.

title: Re-timing mortality risk through individualized modelling of lifespan trajectories.
abstract: There is an urgent global need for affordable, large-scale health screening to enhance preventive care in the ageing population. Using low-cost, non-invasive retinal photographs and leveraging large foundation models, we developed a deep learning-based biomarker, Retinal Mortality Equivalent (RetiME), that directly mapped retinal features to individual mortality risk. Trained on a European cohort and externally validated across three independent external cohorts spanning Southeast Asia, Eurasia and North America, RetiME showed robust associations with all-cause and cause-specific mortality and predicted the incidence of a wide range of systemic and ocular diseases. Crucially, beyond static risk estimation, RetiME re-timed mortality risk by reconstructing personalized lifespan trajectories that were associated with observed mortality outcomes (for example, age of death). Clustering of these trajectories revealed distinct mortality patterns, spanning cancer-predominant, cardiometabolic and neurodegenerative risks, reflecting diverse ageing pathways captured by RetiME. Interpretability analyses showed that RetiME captures diverse biological and retinal features underlying mortality risk. Genome-wide analyses further identified genetic loci associated with RetiME. Collectively, these findings support further evaluation of retinal imaging and trajectory modelling as one component of a comprehensive assessment of mortality risk.

title: TransA-MERFISH reveals divergent post-retinal direction-selective circuits.
abstract: A major goal in neuroscience is to map the transformation of information as it flows through the brain. For example, neurons at many levels of the visual hierarchy are attuned to motion direction 1-5 . However, links between motion-selective computations and cell types at various stages of the visual hierarchy remain unidentified. A key first step in delineating these relationships is to map the wiring diagrams that connect different motion-selective cell types. Here we establish a systematic, cell-type-specific circuit-mapping method, combining an anterograde trans-neuronal fluorescent tracer (mWGA-mCherry) 6 with spatial transcriptomics (multiplexed error-robust fluorescence in situ hybridization (MERFISH)) 7,8 to establish TransA-MERFISH. We used TransA-MERFISH to comprehensively map the synaptic target cell types of four retinal ganglion cell subclasses in superior colliculus (SC) at cell-type resolution. These experiments unexpectedly revealed that retinal on-off direction-selective ganglion cells (ooDSGCs) innervate several direction-selective SC cell types, but do not innervate a SC cell type that was previously reported to display strong direction-selective responses. We validated these results using orthogonal approaches and demonstrated the sensitivity and specificity of TransA-MERFISH. Functional studies of SC activity before and after ablation of retinal direction-selective circuits confirmed that these computationally distinct, ooDSGC-dependent and -independent direction-selective cell types are commingled in SC. Together, our study establishes TransA-MERFISH as a robust framework for mapping wiring diagrams at the cell-type level and uncovers divergent computational mechanisms of motion detection in early visual processing.

title: Hypothalamic volume and cell-type changes in ageing and Alzheimer's disease.
abstract: Alterations in metabolism, stress response, sleep, circadian rhythms and neuroendocrine processes are key features of ageing and neurodegeneration 1,2 . These fundamental processes are regulated by the hypothalamus, yet how its functionally distinct subregions and cell types change during human ageing and Alzheimer's disease (AD) remains largely unexplored. Here we present HypoAD, an atlas of the human hypothalamus in ageing and AD, including high-resolution magnetic resonance imaging from 458 individuals and single-nucleus RNA sequencing of 614,403 nuclei from young participants, patients with AD and age-matched non-dementia control participants. We show that hypothalamic subregions governing metabolism, stress and circadian rhythms are particularly vulnerable, showing notable changes in both volumes and gene expression during ageing and AD. At the molecular level, machine learning models identified the inflammatory response and regulators of circadian rhythms as key cellular predictors of AD. These signatures were reflected in specific cell types: microglia transitioned to a pro-inflammatory state, whereas inhibitory neurons within sleep-regulating and circadian-regulating hypothalamic subregions showed the most profound transcriptional alterations, including disruptions in ligand-receptor interactions and G-protein-coupled receptor signalling. HypoAD provides a high-resolution volumetric map and a transcriptomic atlas of the human hypothalamus in ageing and AD, relating lifestyle and behavioural changes to the relevant volumetric and molecular pathways. In addition, HypoAD provides a framework to investigate hypothalamic dysfunction and establishes a roadmap for targeted interventions aimed at mitigating physiological disruptions to potentially slow disease progression.

title: 4D ultrasound cerebral angiography reveals the hemodynamics of the circle of Willis in primates.
abstract: Noninvasive imaging of hemodynamics in deep cerebral arteries is essential for understanding cerebrovascular regulation, yet remains technically challenging. Existing angiographic techniques provide structural information with limited hemodynamic characterization, whereas transcranial ultrasound is limited by skull-induced attenuation, sensitivity and restricted deep-brain coverage. We introduce four-dimensional ultrasound cerebral angiography, a noninvasive approach using MBs, for in vivo visualization and quantitative assessment of cerebral arterial hemodynamics through the intact skull. We demonstrate imaging of the circle of Willis up to 7 cm deep in nonhuman primates, with quantification of large and small vessels, over 2.5 × 3.5 × 4 cm3 volumes, at 279-Hz volumetric rate for microbubble tracking and 151-µm spatial resolution after 3-min acquisition. This approach reveals flow organization, redistribution dynamics and interindividual variability, establishing four-dimensional ultrasound cerebral angiography as a methodological framework for deep, quantitative transcranial cerebrovascular imaging and provides a foundation for future translational development.

title: Synchrotron X-ray Data of non-diseased and diabetic Human Pancreas Tissue and Islet Segmentation Model.
abstract: Three-dimensional virtual histology using synchrotron radiation micro-computed tomography enables non-destructive visualization of biological tissue microarchitecture with isotropic resolution. To support quantitative studies of human pancreatic morphology, we provide high-resolution 3D X-ray imaging datasets of 55 pancreatic tissue cores from 32 individuals. The collection comprises histologically non-diseased pancreatic tissue from organ donors and non-neoplastic regions of surgical resection specimens from patients with pancreatic cancer, including subgroups with insulin-dependent diabetes or following neoadjuvant chemotherapy. Formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tissue cores with a diameter of 1 mm were imaged at 650 nm isotropic voxel size, yielding a mean effective spatial resolution of 1.66 µm. The cohort includes reconstructed volumes, corresponding immunohistochemistry, clinical metadata, expert-validated annotations, and dataset-specific example 2.5D U-Net models for automated segmentation of islets of Langerhans. A representative co-registered section yielded a Dice similarity coefficient of 0.81 and intersection-over-union of 0.67. This openly accessible, FAIR-compliant resource supports quantitative analysis of endocrine, exocrine, ductal, and stromal architecture and provides a reproducible reference framework for three-dimensional virtual histology of human pancreatic tissue and computational benchmarking.

title: Contextualizing biological heterogeneity in brain structural normativity assessments across the aging continuum with the nearest neighbor normativity framework.
abstract: Background Despite established consensus about the individuality of brain physiology and structural changes, current neuroimaging biomarker paradigms heavily rely on population averages. Here, we define normativity not as a single reference point but as a landscape of permissible configurations arising from diverse physiological manifestations. Methods We introduce the Nearest Neighbor Normativity (N 3 ) framework, designed to parse the natural heterogeneity in brain structural measurements into a diversity-aware biomarker of brain structural decline. Through repeated comparisons within different demographic subgroups, N 3 contextualizes an individual's measurements from several viewpoints along the aging continuum. Relying on local density estimation, it accommodates multiple, shared normative configurations within and across age groups. We use T1-weighted MRI data from 29,883 individuals for training and 7,013 individuals for validation, and benchmark our framework against Brain Age models and Normative Modeling. We evaluate each biomarker's ability to detect neurodegenerative diseases, using them as representative models of atypical brain structural decline. Results In group-level analyses, the N 3 biomarker shows the largest effect sizes in the detection of Mild Cognitive Impairment, Alzheimer's Disease, and Frontotemporal Dementia. Similarly, the N 3 biomarker achieves the highest predictive performance in the classification of neurodegenerative diseases on a single subject level. Notably, the N 3 estimates remain stable across age and robust to compositional changes in the reference sample. Finally, correlation analyses indicate that it captures distinct and complementary aspects of brain structural variation compared to existing approaches. Conclusions Our findings underscore that rethinking normativity assessments to explicitly accommodate natural inter-individual variability can advance our collective efforts toward truly personalized patient care.

Through repeated comparisons within different demographic subgroups, N3 contextualizes an individual's measurements from several viewpoints along the aging continuum. Relying on local density estimation, it accommodates multiple, shared normative configurations within and across age groups. We use T1-weighted MRI data from 29,883 individuals for training and 7,013 individuals for validation, and benchmark our framework against Brain Age models and Normative Modeling. In group-level analyses, the N3 biomarker shows the largest effect sizes in the detection of Mild Cognitive Impairment, Alzheimer's Disease, and Frontotemporal Dementia. title: Activatable hypoxia magnetic resonance imaging for early stratification of radiotherapy response.
abstract: Tumor hypoxia is a major cause of radioresistance and heterogeneous outcomes in radiotherapy (RT). Noninvasive strategies capable of quantifying tumor hypoxia prior to treatment are essential for precision radiotherapy and prognostic stratification. Here, we developed an activatable hypoxia magnetic resonance imaging (ahMRI) nanoprobe (HIG) that translates hypoxia-induced chemical cues into distance-dependent T1 relaxation signals. In a 4T1 breast cancer model, ahMRI demonstrated strong correlations with canonical hypoxia biomarkers from pimonidazole staining. Importantly, pre-treatment ahMRI readouts enabled early discrimination between RT responders and non-responders. Moreover, the change in the signal-to-noise ratio (ΔSNRtumor) value before RT was significantly associated with immune response, including cytotoxic T cell infiltration and M1/M2 macrophage ratios, as well as with tumor growth suppression. These findings highlight the pivotal role of tumor oxygenation in shaping RT efficacy and establish ahMRI as a noninvasive platform for early outcome prediction. This nanoplatform provides a promising avenue for precision-guided RT and individualized cancer treatment.

title: A chemometrically validated discriminative sensing strategy combining biomolecular specificity with data-driven classification of Aβ 1-40 fibrils.
abstract: Achieving selective and sensitive early detection of amyloid-β (Aβ 1-40 ) fibrils, the hallmark of neurodegenerative disease, in the presence of monomers and abundant serum proteins remains a long-standing major challenge for detecting the disease at its preclinical stage. Here, we report a rationally designed fluorescent probe that exhibits a pronounced 585 nm emission enhancement, enabling rapid and selective identification of Aβ 1-40 fibrils with minimal background interference, highlighting its potential for detecting Aβ 1-40 fibrils. The probe shows negligible response toward monomers and common proteins, including human serum albumin (HSA), bovine serum albumin (BSA), and lysozyme, demonstrating high selectivity to Aβ 1-40 fibrils. Mechanistic studies using NMR (Nuclear Magnetic Resonance), FTIR (Fourier-Transform Infrared), CD (Circular Dichroism), and UV-visible spectroscopy reveal that the sensing response arises from specific probe-fibril interactions, including site-dependent binding and π-π stacking with β-sheet structures. CD and FTIR analyses confirm fibril formation and structural integrity, while NMR provides molecular-level evidence of binding-induced perturbations. Chemometric analysis, including principal component analysis (PCA), hierarchical cluster analysis (HCA), k-nearest neighbours (kNN), and partial least squares discriminant analysis (PLS-DA), enables clear classification of fibrils, monomers, and protein interferents with an accuracy of 88.8% and 90%, using fluorescence and absorbance, respectively, validating the potential of the sensing platform. This work establishes a chemometrically validated sensing strategy that combines molecular specificity with data-driven classification via both absorbance and emission spectroscopy, offering a scalable approach for the selective detection of Aβ 1-40 fibrils relevant to Alzheimer's disease (AD) diagnostics.

title: A chromone-based Schiff base derivative for the Cd 2+ -promoted detection of l-proline: validated by DFT, test strip, cotton swab, fish tissue, cellular imaging, and real/herbal water recovery analysis.
abstract: l-proline is a vital stress marker in plants and an indicator of food quality and clinical diagnosis. In this work, we applied a simple chromone-based Schiff base derivative, ( E )-3-(((3-mercapto-5-phenyl-4 H -1,2,4-triazol-4-yl)imino)methyl)-4 H -chromen-4-one (CT), for the Cd 2+ -complex-promoted detection of l-proline in acetonitrile. Within 10 minutes of incubation, the CT-Cd 2+ complex exhibited a strong PL "Turn-On" response in the presence of l-proline among the amino acids, which remained stable between pH 3 and 8. The Job's plot and 1 H NMR (nuclear magnetic resonance)-based titration studies confirmed the 1 : 1 stoichiometry of CT + Cd 2+ to l-proline. Between 0.1 µM and 300 µM, the PL linear dynamic range of CT + Cd 2+ to l-proline was observed, with a limit of detection (LOD) of 141 nM and an association constant ( K a ) of 4.25 × 10 3 M -1 using the Benesi-Hildebrand plot. The mode of binding and the possible photoinduced electron transfer/fluorescence resonance energy transfer (PET/FRET) mechanism are defined by FTIR spectroscopy, 1 H NMR, HR mass spectrometry, and density functional theory (DFT) studies. l-proline sensing by the Cd 2+ complex-promoted technique is corroborated using a test strip, cotton swab, fish tissue, and A549/MCF-7 cellular imaging. l-proline recovery from tap water and herbal water extracts (including Astragalus root (AA), Hedysari root (NAAI), and Coastal Glehnia root (SGC)) ranged from 89.89% to 113.98%. This unique design drives future innovation for l-proline monitoring in biological and environmental samples.

title: π-Bridge engineering of NIR-II fluorophore nanoparticles for high-contrast bioimaging and image-guided surgery.
abstract: Early and accurate diagnosis is essential to timely clinical intervention. Compared with conventional imaging modalities such as magnetic resonance imaging and computed tomography, which remain subject to high cost, inadequate resolution, or ionizing radiation, near-infrared (NIR) fluorescence imaging provides high sensitivity, excellent spatial resolution, and minimal invasiveness. Nevertheless, the development of highly bright NIR fluorophores remains challenging because simultaneous optimization of the molar absorption coefficient (ε) and quantum yield (ΦPL) is difficult to achieve. Here, TPE-HEXOT-DPTQ is rationally designed through π-bridge engineering to balance molecular planarity and distortion. The concurrent optimization of ε and ΦPL endowed TPE-HEXOT-DPTQ nanoparticles with the highest fluorescence brightness, together with exceptional colloidal stability, photostability, and biocompatibility. In vivo NIR-II fluorescence imaging demonstrated remarkable tissue penetration, high spatial resolution, and superior signal-to-background ratios, enabling clear visualization of intricate vascular architectures, including cerebral and auricular vasculature. In subcutaneous breast cancer and orthotopic colorectal tumor models, TPE-HEXOT-DPTQ nanoparticles not only achieved high-contrast tumor imaging but also enabled precise surgical resection of malignant tissues. This work establishes a rational molecular design strategy for high-performance NIR-II fluorophores and highlights their considerable promise for bioimaging and imaging-guided surgery.

title: PFH-loaded hollow iron oxide nanoparticles suppress breast cancer progression through magnetothermal ferroptosis and inhibition of TGF-β1/Smad-driven EMT.
abstract: Breast cancer metastasis remains a major cause of mortality, and epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) is a key process driving tumor progression. Here, we developed perfluorohexane-loaded hollow iron oxide nanoparticles (PFH-HIONs) as a magnetothermal phase-transition platform for image-guided breast cancer therapy. PFH-HIONs were synthesized by vacuum-assisted loading of PFH into hollow iron oxide nanoparticles and characterized for morphology, size, zeta potential, magnetothermal performance, and ultrasound phase-transition behavior. Their antitumor effects were evaluated in MCF-7 cells and in a xenograft model. Ferroptosis-related changes, EMT-associated signaling, macrophage polarization, and immune-related responses were further assessed. PFH-HIONs showed a hollow nanostructure, AMF-responsive heating, and stimulus-triggered ultrasound contrast enhancement. PFH-HIONs combined with AMF reduced MCF-7 cell viability and increased apoptotic cell death. This treatment also induced ferroptosis-related changes, including GPX4 downregulation, 4-HNE and ACSL4 upregulation, and ROS accumulation. In TGF-β1-treated MCF-7 cells, PFH-HION plus AMF suppressed Smad2/3 phosphorylation, reversed EMT-associated protein and transcription factor expression, and these effects were partially attenuated by ferrostatin-1. In addition, PFH-HIONs plus AMF promoted a more pro-inflammatory macrophage phenotype, and conditioned medium from treated tumor cells induced a similar macrophage reprogramming. In vivo , PFH-HIONs plus AMF inhibited tumor growth, increased necrosis, reduced Ki67, and were associated with increased intratumoral infiltration of CD8-positive lymphocyte-like cells and elevated IFN-γ levels, with acceptable short-term biosafety. PFH-HIONs function as a magnetothermal phase-transition nanoplatform with antitumor activity associated with ferroptosis, EMT suppression, and immune-related tumor microenvironment changes, supporting further investigation for image-guided breast cancer therapy.

title: Imageless Robot-assisted Lateral Unicompartmental Knee Arthroplasty.
abstract: Lateral unicompartmental knee arthroplasty (UKA) is a technically demanding procedure because of the unique anatomy, biomechanics, and frequent posterolateral wear of the lateral compartment. Robotic assistance may improve accuracy and reproducibility. To describe a step-by-step technique for imageless robotic-assisted lateral UKA. The procedure is performed through a lateral parapatellar approach using the imageless CORI platform. Key steps include confirmation of isolated lateral osteoarthritis, imageless registration, dynamic ligament assessment, implant planning to address posterolateral wear while preserving constitutional valgus alignment, robotic bone preparation, and final implantation with assessment of alignment and ligament balance. Imageless robotic systems avoid preoperative CT imaging and enable real-time planning based on intraoperative soft-tissue assessment. These features may be particularly advantageous in lateral UKA. Imageless robotic-assisted lateral UKA using the CORI system is a reproducible technique for isolated lateral compartment osteoarthritis. Accurate registration, preservation of native alignment, and dynamic assessment of ligament function are key principles for successful reconstruction.

title: Comparative efficacy of ultrasound versus elbow arthrography in treating Monteggia fractures in young children.
abstract: Purpose This study aims to compare the effectiveness and clinical value of ultrasound-assisted and arthrography-assisted treatment for acute Monteggia fractures in young children. Methods We conducted a retrospective analysis of 40 cases of acute Monteggia fractures in children treated with Kirschner wire or elastic intramedullary nail fixation between April 2020 and April 2025. Among these cases, 19 were treated under arthrography assistance (Group A), and 21 were treated under ultrasound guidance (Group B). We recorded baseline data for both groups, including gender, age, fracture side and type, associated injuries, time from injury to surgery, internal fixation device, fluoroscopy time, surgical duration, follow-up duration, and internal fixation removal time. Postoperative X-ray examination was performed to assess the quality of fracture reduction. Results Fluoroscopy time and surgical duration in Group B were significantly lower than in Group A (P < 0.05). Based on the evaluation criteria for assessing reduction quality, 17 cases were graded excellent, and 2 were considered good in Group A, while in Group B, 20 cases were deemed excellent and 1 was considered good. At the final follow-up, there was no significant difference in the range of elbow flexion, extension, pronation, and supination between the affected limbs of Group A and Group B (P > 0.05). Conclusion Ultrasound not only saves surgical time and reduces intraoperative radiation exposure for the patients but also enables the exploration of peripheral nerves, vessels, and soft tissue compressions.

title: Surgical versus Conservative Treatment of Isolated Posterior Malleolar Fractures: Clinical, Radiological, and Pedobarographic Outcomes.
abstract: Background Optimal management of isolated posterior malleolar (PM) fractures remains controversial, particularly regarding the influence of fracture fragment size on treatment selection and outcomes. Purpose To compare clinical, radiological, and pedobarographic outcomes of surgically and conservatively treated isolated PM fractures and to assess the effect of fracture fragment size on outcomes. Study design Retrospective observational study. Methods Patients with isolated PM fractures were divided into surgical and conservative groups. Fracture classification and fragment size were assessed using plain radiographs and computed tomography (CT). Clinical evaluation included the American Orthopaedic Foot and Ankle Society (AOFAS) score, visual analog scale (VAS) for pain, ankle range of motion, and radiographic osteoarthritis graded by the Kellgren-Lawrence classification. Static and dynamic pedobarographic analyses were performed. Subgroup analyses were conducted according to CT-measured fragment size. Results Thirty patients were included. CT measurements revealed significantly larger fragment sizes than plain radiographs (p < 0.001). Surgical treatment was associated with higher AOFAS scores and lower VAS pain scores than conservative treatment in this non-randomized cohort. In the subgroup with fragments involving more than 25% of the articular surface, surgically treated patients had higher AOFAS scores and lower pain scores; this exploratory comparison included only 10 surgical and 4 conservatively treated patients. No consistent pedobarographic differences were detected, although these exploratory comparisons were likely underpowered. Contralateral hindfoot pressure differed in one comparison. Conclusion Surgical treatment was associated with higher functional scores and lower pain levels in this small, non-randomized cohort. The apparent difference in the > 25% subgroup is exploratory and requires confirmation in larger studies. CT-based assessment provided more detailed evaluation of fracture morphology and may assist treatment planning.

title: [The infected diabetic foot syndrome - diagnosis, treatment, and interdisciplinary care].
abstract: Abstract Diabetic foot syndrome (DFS) is one of the most severe long-term complications of diabetes mellitus and represents the leading cause of non-traumatic lower extremity amputations in industrialized nations. While the pathogenesis of foot ulcerations is primarily driven by a combination of diabetic polyneuropathy and peripheral arterial disease (PAD), secondary infections are frequently the main trigger for critical tissue loss. Consequently, these infections necessitate urgent inpatient admission and often result in major amputations as a last resort.The diagnosis of a diabetic foot infection is fundamentally based on clinical presentation. Key components for successful management include the early detection of underlying osteomyelitis, the identification of relevant perfusion deficits, and the immediate initiation of a structured, multimodal therapy regimen. This standard regimen comprises targeted surgical debridement, consistent pressure offloading, pathogen-specific antimicrobial therapy, and prompt vascular revascularization. Due to the highly complex underlying pathophysiology, patients with advanced disease stages benefit substantially from organized interdisciplinary care involving diabetologists, specialized podiatric surgeons, vascular surgeons, interventional radiologists, clinical infectious disease specialists, and orthopedic shoemakers. This comprehensive article provides a highly practice-oriented overview of the modern diagnosis and therapeutic management of the infected diabetic foot, strictly aligned with the current recommendations of the German Diabetes Society (DDG) and the International Working Group on the Diabetic Foot (IWGDF).

title: Technology-Enabled Skin Longevity Optimization.
abstract: Aims and Backgrounds: Facial aging is a multifactorial process involving cellular senescence, ultraviolet damage, and structural decline across the epidermis, dermis, subcutaneous fat, and superficial musculoaponeurotic system. Contemporary rejuvenation has evolved beyond surgical repositioning toward biologically targeted cutaneous optimization. Technology Energy-based technologies including laser photothermolysis, radiofrequency-mediated dermal thermomodulation, microfocused ultrasound, and emerging microwave and cryobiologic modalities induce controlled tissue injury that activates wound-healing pathways, fibroblast proliferation, and extracellular matrix remodeling. Techniques Regenerative strategies including microneedling-assisted mechanotransduction, platelet-derived biologics, autologous fat grafting, collagen biostimulators, and extracellular vesicle therapies provide biologically oriented tissue restoration through paracrine signaling and matrix synthesis. Current and Future Development: Artificial intelligence applications in facial phenotyping, treatment planning, and outcome assessment are emerging. Future directions include senescence-targeting therapies and precision-based multimodal protocols. Conclusions and clinical relevance Multimodal treatment sequencing addressing multiple anatomical layers represents the contemporary standard. Integration of device-based technologies with regenerative adjuncts enables biologically informed, individualized facial rejuvenation.

title: Knowledge, Compliance, and Associated Factors of Radiation Protection Adherence Among Dental Students, Interns, and Dentists: A Cross-Sectional Study.
abstract: Objectives Dental radiography is essential for diagnosis and treatment planning, but exposure to ionizing radiation requires strict adherence to radiation protection principles. This study evaluated radiation protection knowledge, self-reported compliance, and their associated factors among dental students, interns, and dentists. Materials and methods A cross-sectional study included 136 participants (86.1% response rate). A content-reviewed bilingual questionnaire assessed 7 knowledge items (6 scored in the composite knowledge score) and 12 self-reported compliance items. Pilot testing, translation, content validity (scale-level average content validity index [S-CVI/Ave] = 0.91), and internal consistency (α = 0.78; Kuder-Richardson Formula 20 [KR-20] = 0.70) were evaluated. Multivariable ordinary least squares regression examined factors associated with compliance using SPSS 27 and Python software. Results The composite knowledge score was 0.804; the pediatric radiation protection item had a correct-response rate of 54.4% (single-item assessment). Mean compliance was 3.09/4. Composite knowledge score was independently associated with self-reported compliance ( B = 1.092, 95% confidence interval: 0.817-1.366, p < 0.001). Compliance was significantly lower among Year 5 students and interns than among Year 3 students ( p = 0.037 and p = 0.005, respectively), whereas gender and the remaining training-level contrasts were not significant ( R 2 = 0.360). Knowledge showed a moderate-to-strong positive correlation with compliance ( rₛ = 0.528, p < 0.001). Exploratory analyses indicated a stronger knowledge-compliance association among more advanced trainees (Year 5, interns, and dentists/faculty) than among earlier-year students. The largest compliance gaps involved X-ray image repetition frequency, use of protective shielding devices, and motion-restraining tools. Conclusion Composite knowledge score was independently associated with self-reported compliance, and adjusted compliance was lower among Year 5 students and interns than among Year 3 students. However, the cross-sectional design and reliance on self-reported data preclude causal interpretation. Lower compliance was observed for X-ray image repetition frequency, protective shielding devices, and motion-restraining tools. These findings support competency-based training and curriculum review, but recommendations remain exploratory and require confirmation in larger multi-institutional prospective studies.

title: Radiographic manifestations of pneumatosis intestinalis and construction of an AI-assisted diagnostic system.
abstract: Pneumatosis intestinalis (PI) has a wide range of etiologies, and the imaging differentiation between benign and ischemic PI is difficult, leading to a high risk of missed diagnosis. This study systematically summarizes the CT (Computed Tomography) imaging manifestations of PI and constructs an AI (Artificial Intelligence)-assisted diagnostic model that integrates multidimensional features. This study retrospectively collected CT and x-ray data from 612 patients with PI (398 benign and 214 ischemic cases) from three tertiary hospitals, and included an external validation set of 106 cases. Imaging analysis established a five-level PI-CT severity scoring system based on gas morphology, distribution, portal venous gas (PVG), intestinal wall enhancement, mesenteric edema, and ascites. The AI system adopted a two-level architecture: The first level used EfficientNet-B3 for rapid screening on x-ray films; the second level used 3D nnU-Net (No-new-Net) to segment intestinal wall gas, and then fused the data through a three-branch network (gas morphology, accompanying signs, and clinical metadata) via cross-attention to output the probability of ischemic PI. In the internal test set, the model achieved an AUC (Area Under the Curve) of 0.947 for ischemic PI (sensitivity 91.3%, specificity 93.6%), significantly outperforming senior radiologists (AUC = 0.876); the AUC on the external validation set was 0.931. SHapley Additive exPlanations analysis showed that PVG and blood lactate were the most important predictors. This two-tiered AI system can significantly improve the early identification of the causes of critical PI, providing a reliable method for intelligent diagnosis of emergency imaging.

title: Foundation models in radiology: Development, applications, and future impact.
abstract: Foundation models represent a major evolution in artificial intelligence, enabling models pretrained on large, diverse datasets to be adapted to a wide range of downstream tasks with substantially less task-specific training data. In radiology, advances in transformer architectures, self-supervised learning, and vision-language models have created new opportunities to integrate image and text understanding within versatile artificial intelligence systems. Potential applications span the radiology workflow and include image interpretation, automated report drafting and summarization, clinical decision support, information retrieval, and development of specialized task-specific models. Among these, AI-assisted report generation represents a particularly promising near-term application, although current performance supports a role as a drafting assistant rather than an autonomous replacement for radiologists. Important barriers to clinical adoption remain, including limitations in model performance, regulatory requirements, and the risk of automation bias. In the near term, foundation models may have their greatest impact by augmenting radiologists and accelerating the development of specialized artificial intelligence applications rather than replacing existing systems or physician expertise. This review describes the technological advances underlying foundation models, highlights their current and emerging applications in radiology, examines key risks and implementation challenges, and considers their potential impact on the future practice of radiology.

title: The impact of artificial intelligence on peer review in radiology journals.
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming radiology research and is progressively influencing the scholarly publication process itself. Large language models (LLMs) are being increasingly used for manuscript writing. At the other end of the spectrum, AI can assist with manuscript screening, statistical and methodological assessment, language editing, reference checking, reviewer selection, and the generation of peer-review comments. LLMs have the potential to improve the efficiency of journal review by reducing repetitive tasks and helping reviewers identify reporting deficiencies. However, their integration also introduces substantial concerns regarding confidentiality, hallucination, bias, reproducibility, authorship, accountability, and manipulation of the peer-review process. In this article, the authors examine the potential benefits and limitations of AI-assisted peer review in radiology journals and propose a framework in which AI serves as a controlled decision-support tool rather than an autonomous reviewer. Human reviewers and editors should retain responsibility for scientific judgment, confidentiality, and final editorial decisions. This approach harnesses AI's efficiency while maintaining accountability.
